They also ascribed divinity, and built temples, to mere accidents and qualities — such as Time, Night, Day, Peace, Concord, Love, Strife, Virtue, Honor, Health, Rust, Fever, and the like — which, when they prayed for them or against them, they prayed to as if there were ghosts of those names hovering over their heads, letting fall or withholding the good or evil for or against which they prayed. They also invoked their own wit, by the name of the Muses; their own ignorance, by the name of Fortune; their own lust, by the name of Cupid; their own rage, by the name of the Furies; their own private parts, by the name of Priapus; and they attributed their pollutions to Incubi and Succubae — so that there was nothing a poet could introduce as a character in his poem that they did not make into either a god or a devil.

The same authors of the religion of the Gentiles, observing the second ground of religion — namely men's ignorance of causes, and their consequent readiness to attribute their fortune to causes on which there was no apparent dependence — took the opportunity to foist on this ignorance, in place of secondary causes, a kind of second-rank, ministering gods: ascribing fertility to Venus, the arts to Apollo, subtlety and craft to Mercury, tempests and storms to Aeolus, and other effects to other gods — so that among the heathen there was almost as great a variety of gods as of occupations.

And to the worship which men naturally thought fit to use toward their gods — namely oblations, prayers, thanks, and the rest already named — the same legislators of the Gentiles added images of them, both in painting and in sculpture, so that the more ignorant sort (that is, the greater part of the people), thinking that the gods the images represented were really included, as it were housed within them, might stand all the more in fear of them. They endowed them with lands, houses, officers, and revenues, set apart from all other human uses — that is, consecrated and made holy to these idols — such as caverns, groves, woods, mountains, and whole islands. And they attributed to them not only shapes (of men, of beasts, of monsters), but also the faculties and passions of men and beasts: sense, speech, sex, lust, generation (and this not only by mixing with one another to propagate the kind of gods, but also by mixing with men and women to beget mongrel gods, mere lodgers in heaven, such as Bacchus, Hercules, and others); besides anger, revenge, and other passions of living creatures, and the actions proceeding from them — fraud, theft, adultery, sodomy, and any vice that may be taken either as an effect of power or as a cause of pleasure; and all such vices as, among men, are considered to be against law rather than against honor.

Lastly, to the prognostics of the time to come (which are naturally only conjectures based on past experience, and supernaturally divine revelation), the same authors of the religion of the Gentiles added, partly on pretended experience and partly on pretended revelation, innumerable other superstitious forms of divination. They made men believe they might find their fortunes sometimes in the ambiguous or senseless answers of the priests at Delphi, Delos, Ammon, and other famous oracles — answers made ambiguous by design, so that the event could be claimed either way, or made absurd by the intoxicating vapor of the place, which is very common in sulphurous caverns. Sometimes in the leaves of the Sibyls (whose prophecies — like those perhaps of Nostradamus, for the surviving fragments seem to be of later invention — had some books of repute in the time of the Roman Republic). Sometimes in the meaningless speeches of madmen, supposed to be possessed by a divine spirit (which possession they called Enthusiasm); and these kinds of foretelling were called Theomancy, or prophecy. Sometimes in the aspect of the stars at one's birth, which was called Horoscopy and counted a branch of judicial astrology. Sometimes in their own hopes and fears, called Thumomancy, or presage. Sometimes in the predictions of witches, who claimed to confer with the dead — which is called Necromancy, Conjuring, and Witchcraft, and is nothing but trickery and collusive fraud. Sometimes in the chance flight or feeding of birds, called Augury. Sometimes in the entrails of a sacrificed beast, which was Aruspicina. Sometimes in dreams. Sometimes in the croaking of ravens, or the chattering of birds. Sometimes in the features of the face, which was called Metoposcopy; or by Palmistry, in the lines of the hand; in chance words, called Omina. Sometimes in monsters or unusual accidents — such as eclipses, comets, rare meteors, earthquakes, floods, strange births, and the like — which they called Portenta and Ostenta because they were thought to portend or foreshow some great calamity to come. Sometimes in mere lottery, like heads or tails (Cross and Pile), counting holes in a sieve, dipping into verses of Homer and Virgil, and innumerable other empty conceits. So easily are men drawn to believe anything from such men as have gained credit with them, and who can with gentleness and dexterity take hold of their fear and ignorance.

[The Designs Of The Authors Of The Religion Of The Heathen.] And therefore the first founders and legislators of commonwealths among the Gentiles, whose aims were only to keep the people in obedience and peace, have everywhere taken care: First, to imprint in their minds a belief that the precepts they gave concerning religion should not be thought to come from their own invention but from the dictates of some god or other spirit — or else that they themselves were of a higher nature than mere mortals — so that their laws might more easily be received. Thus Numa Pompilius pretended to receive the ceremonies he established among the Romans from the nymph Egeria; the first king and founder of the kingdom of Peru pretended that he and his wife were children of the Sun; and Mahomet, to set up his new religion, pretended to have conferences with the Holy Ghost, in the form of a dove. Second, they took care to have it believed that the same things were displeasing to the gods which were forbidden by the laws. Third, to prescribe ceremonies, supplications, sacrifices, and festivals, by which they were to believe the anger of the gods might be appeased; and that bad success in war, great epidemics, earthquakes, and every man's private misery came from the anger of the gods, and their anger from the neglect of their worship, or from forgetting or mistaking some point of the required ceremonies. And although among the ancient Romans men were not forbidden to deny what the poets wrote of the pains and pleasures after this life — which many of great authority and gravity in that state openly derided in their public speeches — yet that belief was always more cherished than its opposite.

And by these and other such institutions, they obtained, in service of their end (which was the peace of the commonwealth), this: that the common people in their misfortunes, blaming neglect or error in their ceremonies, or their own disobedience to the laws, were less apt to mutiny against their governors. And being entertained with the pomp and pastime of festivals and public games made in honor of the gods, they needed nothing else but bread to keep them from discontent, murmuring, and uprising against the state. And therefore the Romans, having conquered the greatest part of the then-known world, made no scruple of tolerating any religion whatsoever in the City of Rome itself, unless it had something in it inconsistent with their civil government. Nor do we read that any religion was forbidden there except that of the Jews, who (being the peculiar kingdom of God) thought it unlawful to acknowledge subjection to any mortal king or state whatsoever. And thus you see how the religion of the Gentiles was a part of their policy.

[The True Religion, And The Laws Of God's Kingdom The Same.] But where God himself, by supernatural revelation, planted religion, there he also made for himself a peculiar kingdom, and gave laws — not only of behavior toward himself but also toward one another. And thereby in the kingdom of God, policy and the civil laws are a part of religion, and so the distinction between temporal and spiritual dominion has no place there. It is true that God is king of all the earth; yet he may be king of a particular, chosen nation. For there is no more incongruity in this than that one who holds the general command of the whole army should also have his own particular regiment or company. God is king of all the earth by his power, but of his chosen people he is king by covenant. But I have assigned another place in the following discourse to speak more fully of the kingdom of God, both by nature and by covenant.

From the way religion is propagated, it is not hard to understand the causes by which it dissolves back into its first seeds or principles — which are only an opinion of a deity and of powers invisible and supernatural. These can never be so abolished out of human nature but that new religions may once again spring out of them, by the cultivation of such men as are held in repute for that purpose.

For since all formed religion is founded at first upon the faith that a multitude has in some one person, whom they believe not only to be a wise man, laboring to procure their happiness, but also a holy man, to whom God himself vouchsafes to declare his will supernaturally, it follows necessarily that when those who govern religion come to have their wisdom suspected, or their sincerity, or their love; or when they are unable to show any plausible token of divine revelation, the religion they would uphold must also be suspected, and (without the fear of the civil sword) contradicted and rejected.

What takes away the reputation of wisdom in someone who forms a religion, or adds to it once it has been formed, is the demand that men believe contradictions. For both sides of a contradiction cannot possibly be true; and so to enjoin belief in them is a sign of ignorance, which exposes the author in that, and discredits him in everything else he may propose as coming from supernatural revelation. A man may indeed have revelation of many things above natural reason, but of nothing against it.

What takes away the reputation of sincerity is the doing or saying of such things as appear to be signs that what they require other men to believe is not believed by themselves. All such doings or sayings are therefore called Scandalous, because they are stumbling-blocks that make men fall in the way of religion: injustice, cruelty, profaneness, avarice, and luxury. For who can believe that someone who ordinarily does the kinds of things that proceed from any of these roots really believes there is any such invisible power to be feared as he uses to frighten other men over lesser faults?

What takes away the reputation of love is the discovery of private ends — as when the belief they require of others tends, or seems to tend, to acquiring dominion, riches, dignity, or secure pleasure for themselves alone or especially. For what men gain advantage by for themselves, they are thought to do for their own sake, and not out of love for others.

Lastly, the testimony men can give of a divine calling can be nothing other than the working of miracles; or true prophecy (which is also a miracle); or extraordinary felicity. And therefore, in addition to those points of religion that have been received from people who did such miracles, the points added by those who do not approve their calling by any miracle gain no greater belief than what the custom and laws of the places where they were brought up have instilled in them. For as in natural things men of judgment require natural signs and arguments, so in supernatural things they require supernatural signs (which are miracles) before they assent inwardly and from their hearts.

All these causes of the weakening of men's faith are clearly apparent in the following examples. First, we have the example of the children of Israel, who, when Moses (who had proved his calling to them by miracles and by the happy leading of them out of Egypt) was absent only forty days, revolted from the worship of the true God that he had commended to them, and setting up (Exod. 32:1,2) a Golden Calf for their God, relapsed into the idolatry of the Egyptians, from whom they had been so recently delivered. And again, after Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the generation that had seen the great works of God in Israel were dead (Judges 2:11), another generation arose and served Baal. So that, miracles failing, faith also failed.

Again, when the sons of Samuel (1 Sam. 8:3), having been appointed by their father as judges in Beersheba, took bribes and judged unjustly, the people of Israel refused any longer to have God as their king in any way different from how he was king of other peoples, and therefore cried out to Samuel to choose them a king after the manner of the nations. So that, justice failing, faith also failed — to the point that they deposed their God from reigning over them.

And whereas in the planting of the Christian religion the oracles ceased in every part of the Roman Empire, and the number of Christians increased wonderfully every day and in every place by the preaching of the Apostles and Evangelists, a great part of that success may reasonably be attributed to the contempt into which the priests of the Gentiles of that time had brought themselves, by their uncleanness, avarice, and dealings between princes. Also the religion of the Church of Rome was, partly for the same reason, abolished in England and in many other parts of Christendom — so that the failing of virtue in the pastors makes faith fail in the people. And partly it was abolished because of the bringing of the philosophy and doctrine of Aristotle into religion by the schoolmen, from which there arose so many contradictions and absurdities that they brought the clergy into a reputation both of ignorance and of fraudulent intention, inclining people to revolt from them — either against the will of their own princes, as in France and Holland, or with their will, as in England.

Lastly, among the points the Church of Rome declares necessary for salvation, there are so many manifestly to the advantage of the Pope and of his spiritual subjects residing in the territories of other Christian princes, that were it not for the mutual rivalry of those princes, they might without war or trouble exclude all foreign authority as easily as it has been excluded in England. For who is there that does not see whose benefit it serves to have it believed: that a king has no authority from Christ unless a bishop crowns him? That a king, if he is a priest, cannot marry? That whether a prince is born in lawful marriage or not must be judged by authority from Rome? That subjects may be freed from their allegiance if, by the Court of Rome, the king is judged a heretic? That a king (like Chilperic of France) may be deposed by a pope (like Pope Zachary) for no cause, and his kingdom given to one of his subjects? That the clergy and the regulars, in whatever country, shall be exempt from the jurisdiction of their king in criminal cases? Or who does not see to whose profit accrue the fees of private masses, and the takings of purgatory, with other signs of private interest — enough to mortify the most lively faith, if (as I said) the civil magistrate and custom did not sustain it more than any opinion they have of the sanctity, wisdom, or probity of their teachers? So that I may attribute all the changes of religion in the world to one and the same cause: displeasing priests — and not only among Catholics, but even in that church which has presumed most of reformation.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII. Of the Naturall Condition of Mankind, as Concerning Their Felicity, and Misery
paragraphs: Nature has made men so equal in the faculties of body and mind that, although one man may sometimes be clearly stronger in body or quicker of mind than another, when everything is reckoned together the difference between one man and another is not so considerable that one man can claim for himself any benefit to which another may not equally lay claim. As for bodily strength, the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret scheming or by joining with others who are in the same danger as himself.

And as for the faculties of the mind (setting aside the arts grounded on words, and especially that skill of proceeding by general and infallible rules called Science — which very few men have, and they only in a few things, as it is not an inborn faculty nor acquired, like Prudence, while we are looking after something else) — I find a still greater equality among men than there is in strength. For Prudence is just Experience, which equal time bestows equally on all men in those things to which they apply themselves equally. What may perhaps make such equality seem incredible is only a vain conceit of one's own wisdom, which almost every man thinks he has in a greater degree than the common sort — that is, than everyone but himself and a few others whom he approves, either because of their fame or because their opinions agree with his own. For such is the nature of men that, although they may acknowledge many others to be more clever, more eloquent, or more learned, they will hardly believe there are many as wise as themselves. They see their own wit at hand, and other men's at a distance. But this proves rather that men are equal in this point than unequal. For there is ordinarily no greater sign of the equal distribution of anything than that every man is contented with his share.

From this equality of ability arises equality of hope in attaining our ends. And therefore if any two men desire the same thing, which nevertheless they cannot both enjoy, they become enemies. And in pursuit of their end (which is principally their own preservation, and sometimes only their pleasure), they endeavor to destroy or subdue one another. From this it comes about that, where an invader has nothing more to fear than the single power of one other man, if one person plants, sows, builds, or settles on a convenient spot, others may probably be expected to come with their forces combined to dispossess him and to deprive him not only of the fruit of his labor but also of his life or liberty. And the invader, in turn, is in the like danger from another.

And given this mutual distrust, there is no way for any man to secure himself that is as reasonable as Anticipation — that is, by force or cunning to master the persons of all the men he can, until he sees no other power great enough to endanger him. This is no more than his own preservation requires, and is generally allowed. Also, since there are some who take pleasure in contemplating their own power in acts of conquest — pursuing it further than their security requires — if others, who would otherwise be glad to be at ease within modest bounds, were not by invasion to increase their power, they would not be able for long to subsist by standing only on the defensive. Consequently, such enlargement of dominion over other men, being necessary for a man's preservation, must be allowed him.

Again, men take no pleasure (but on the contrary a great deal of grief) in keeping company where there is no power able to overawe them all. For every man expects his companion to value him at the same rate he sets upon himself, and at any sign of contempt or undervaluing he naturally endeavors, so far as he dares (which, among those who have no common power to keep them in quiet, is far enough to make them destroy each other), to extort a greater valuation from those who scorn him — by damaging them, and from others by his example.
So in the nature of man we find three principal causes of quarrel. First, Competition; second, Diffidence; third, Glory.

The first makes men invade for gain; the second, for safety; and the third, for reputation. The first use violence to make themselves masters of other men's persons, wives, children, and cattle; the second, to defend them; the third, for trifles — a word, a smile, a different opinion, and any other sign of low estimation, whether directly aimed at their own persons or by reflection at their kindred, their friends, their nation, their profession, or their name.

From this it is plain that during the time men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition called War, and such a war as is of every man against every man (a war of all against all). For WAR consists not in battle only, or the act of fighting, but in a stretch of time in which the will to contend by battle is sufficiently known. And therefore the notion of Time is to be considered in the nature of war, as it is in the nature of weather. For just as the nature of foul weather lies not in a shower or two of rain but in an inclination toward it over many days together, so the nature of war consists not in actual fighting but in the known disposition to fight, during all the time there is no assurance to the contrary. All other time is PEACE.

Whatever therefore follows from a time of war, where every man is enemy to every man, the same follows from any time in which men live without any other security than what their own strength and their own invention will furnish them with. In such a condition there is no place for industry, because the fruit of it is uncertain — and consequently no cultivation of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no convenient building; no instruments for moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and, which is worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death; and the life of man, “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.”

It may seem strange to someone who has not weighed these things carefully that nature should thus pull men apart and make them apt to invade and destroy one another. He may therefore, not trusting this inference drawn from the passions, desire perhaps to have it confirmed by experience. Let him then consider with himself: when he takes a journey, he arms himself and seeks to travel well accompanied; when he goes to sleep, he locks his doors; even in his own house he locks his chests; and this when he knows there are laws and public officers, armed, to avenge any injury done to him. What opinion does he have of his fellow subjects when he rides armed? Of his fellow citizens when he locks his doors? And of his children and servants when he locks his chests? Does he not accuse mankind as much by his actions as I do by my words? But neither of us accuses man's nature in it. The desires and other passions of man are in themselves no sin. Nor are the actions that proceed from those passions, until they know a law that forbids them — which, until laws are made, they cannot know. Nor can any law be made until they have agreed on the person who shall make it.

It may perhaps be thought that there never was such a time, nor such a condition of war as this; and I believe it was never generally so over all the world. But there are many places where men live so now. For the savage people in many parts of America, except for the government of small families (whose concord depends on natural lust), have no government at all, and live to this day in that brutish manner I described before. In any case, what kind of life there would be where there was no common power to fear may be seen from the kind of life men who have formerly lived under a peaceful government degenerate into during a civil war.

But even if there had never been any time when individual men were in a condition of war against one another, in all times kings and persons of sovereign authority, because of their independence, are in continual jealousies, and in the state and posture of gladiators — their weapons pointing and their eyes fixed on one another. That is, their forts, garrisons, and guns are on the frontiers of their kingdoms, and they keep continual spies upon their neighbors, which is a posture of war. But because by these means they uphold the industry of their subjects, the misery that accompanies the liberty of private men does not follow from it.

From this war of every man against every man, this also follows: that nothing can be unjust. The notions of right and wrong, of justice and injustice, have no place there. Where there is no common power, there is no law; where there is no law, there is no injustice. Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues. Justice and injustice are not faculties of either the body or the mind. If they were, they might be in a man who was alone in the world, just as his senses and passions are. They are qualities that relate to men in society, not in solitude. It also follows from the same condition that there is no property, no dominion, no Mine and Thine distinct — only what each man can get, and for as long as he can keep it. And so much for the bad condition that man is actually placed in by mere nature, though with a possibility of coming out of it, lying partly in the passions and partly in his reason.

The passions that incline men to peace are: fear of death; desire of such things as are necessary for a comfortable life; and a hope of obtaining them by their industry. And reason suggests convenient articles of peace, on which men may be brought to agreement. These articles are what are otherwise called the Laws of Nature, of which I shall speak more particularly in the two following chapters.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV. Of the First and Second Naturall Lawes, and of Contracts
paragraphs: The RIGHT OF NATURE, which writers commonly call Jus Naturale, is the liberty each man has to use his own power as he himself wills, for the preservation of his own nature — that is, of his own life — and consequently of doing anything which, in his own judgment and reason, he conceives to be the aptest means to it.

By LIBERTY is understood, according to the proper meaning of the word, the absence of external impediments. These impediments may often take away part of a man's power to do what he would, but they cannot hinder him from using the power left to him according as his judgment and reason direct.

A LAW OF NATURE (Lex Naturalis) is a precept or general rule, found out by reason, by which a man is forbidden to do what is destructive of his life, or what takes away the means of preserving it, and to omit that by which he thinks it may be best preserved. Those who write on this subject usually confuse Jus and Lex — Right and Law — yet they ought to be distinguished. For RIGHT consists in the liberty to do or to forbear, whereas LAW determines and binds to one of these. So Law and Right differ as much as obligation and liberty, which in one and the same matter are inconsistent.

And because the condition of man (as has been declared in the previous chapter) is a condition of war of everyone against everyone — in which everyone is governed by his own reason, and there is nothing he can use that may not be a help in preserving his life against his enemies — it follows that in such a condition every man has a right to everything, even to one another's body. And therefore, as long as this natural right of every man to everything endures, there can be no security for any man (however strong or wise he may be) of living out the time which nature ordinarily allows men to live.

And consequently it is a precept, or general rule of reason, “That every man, ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre.” The first branch of this rule contains the first and fundamental law of nature, which is: “To seek Peace, and follow it.” The second contains the sum of the right of nature, which is: “By all means we can, to defend our selves.”

From this fundamental law of nature, by which men are commanded to endeavor peace, is derived this second law: “That a man be willing, when others are so too, as farre-forth, as for Peace, and defence of himselfe he shall think it necessary, to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men, as he would allow other men against himselfe.” For as long as every man holds this right — of doing anything he likes — so long are all men in the condition of war. But if other men will not lay down their right as well as he, then there is no reason for anyone to divest himself of his, for that would be exposing himself to prey (which no man is bound to do) rather than disposing himself toward peace. This is that law of the Gospel: “Whatsoever you require that others should do to you, that do ye to them.” And that law of all men: “Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris” (Do not do to another what you would not want done to you).

To LAY DOWN a man's right to anything is to divest himself of the liberty of hindering another from the benefit of his own right to the same. For he who renounces or passes away his right does not give to any other man a right which that other did not have before — because there is nothing to which every man did not have a right by nature — but only steps out of the other's way, so that the other may enjoy his own original right without hindrance from him (though not without hindrance from another). So the effect that accrues to one man from another's relinquishing his right is just so much diminution of impediments to the use of his own original right.

A right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it, or by transferring it to another. By simply RENOUNCING it, when a man does not care to whom the benefit of it accrues. By TRANSFERRING it, when he intends the benefit to some particular person or persons. And when a man has in either manner abandoned or granted away his right, he is then said to be OBLIGED, or BOUND, not to hinder those to whom such right is granted or abandoned from the benefit of it; and to do so is his DUTY, not to make void that voluntary act of his own. Any such hindrance is INJUSTICE, and INJURY, as being Sine Jure (without right) — the right having been previously renounced or transferred. So injury or injustice, in the controversies of the world, is somewhat like what in the disputations of scholars is called absurdity. For just as it is called an absurdity there to contradict what one maintained at the beginning, so in the world it is called injustice and injury voluntarily to undo what from the beginning one had voluntarily done. The way by which a man either simply renounces or transfers his right is a declaration, or signification, by some voluntary and sufficient sign or signs, that he does so renounce or transfer, or has so renounced or transferred it, to the person who accepts it. And these signs are either words only, or actions only, or (as most often happens) both words and actions. They are the BONDS by which men are bound and obliged: bonds that have their strength not from their own nature (for nothing is more easily broken than a man's word), but from fear of some evil consequence on the rupture.

Whenever a man transfers his right or renounces it, it is either in consideration of some right reciprocally transferred to him, or for some other good he hopes for by it. For it is a voluntary act, and the object of every voluntary act of a man is some good to himself. And therefore there are some rights which no man can be understood, by any words or other signs, to have abandoned or transferred. First, a man cannot lay down the right to resist those who assault him by force to take away his life, because he cannot be understood to aim by this at any good to himself. The same may be said of wounds, chains, and imprisonment — both because there is no benefit following from such patience (as there is from the patience of letting another be wounded or imprisoned), and because a man cannot tell, when he sees men proceed against him by violence, whether they intend his death or not. And lastly, the motive and end for which this renouncing and transferring of right is introduced is nothing else but the security of a man's person — in his life, and in the means of preserving life so as not to be weary of it. And therefore if a man by words or other signs seems to despoil himself of the end for which those signs were intended, he is not to be understood as if he meant it, or that it was his will, but that he was ignorant of how such words and actions were to be interpreted.
The mutual transferring of right is what men call CONTRACT.

There is a difference between transferring the right to the thing and transferring (or tradition, that is, delivery of) the thing itself. For the thing may be delivered together with the transfer of the right — as in buying and selling for ready money, or in the exchange of goods or lands — and it may be delivered some time afterward.

Again, one of the contractors may deliver the thing contracted for on his part, and leave the other to perform his part at some specified later time, being meanwhile trusted; and then the contract on his part is called PACT, or COVENANT. Or both parties may contract now, to perform hereafter; in which cases the one who is to perform in the time to come, being trusted, his performance is called keeping of promise, or faith; and the failure to perform (if it is voluntary) is called violation of faith.

When the transferring of right is not mutual, but one of the parties transfers in hope of gaining by it friendship or service from another (or from his friends), or in hope of gaining the reputation of charity or magnanimity, or to free his mind from the pain of compassion, or in hope of reward in heaven — this is not contract, but GIFT, FREE-GIFT, GRACE: words that signify one and the same thing.

Signs of contract are either express, or by inference. Express, when they are words spoken with understanding of what they mean. Such words are either of present or past time — as “I give, I grant, I have given, I have granted, I will that this be yours” — or of the future, as “I will give, I will grant.” Words of the future are called Promise.

Signs by inference are sometimes the consequence of words, sometimes of silence, sometimes of actions, sometimes of forbearing an action. Generally, a sign by inference of any contract is whatever sufficiently shows the will of the contractor.

Words alone, if they are of time to come and contain a bare promise, are an insufficient sign of a free gift, and therefore not binding. For if they are of the future, like “Tomorrow I will give,” they are a sign that I have not given yet — and consequently that my right is not transferred, but remains until I transfer it by some other act. But if the words are of present or past time, such as “I have given, or do give, to be delivered tomorrow,” then my tomorrow's right is given away today; and that by the force of the words, even if there were no other indication of my will. There is a great difference in the meaning of these words: Volo hoc tuum esse cras, and Cras dabo — that is, between “I will that this be thine tomorrow,” and “I will give it to thee tomorrow.” The phrase “I will,” in the former, signifies an act of the will present; in the latter, it signifies a promise of an act of the will to come. So the former words, being of the present, transfer a future right; the latter, being of the future, transfer nothing. But if there are other signs of the will to transfer a right besides words, then, even though the gift is free, the right may be understood to pass by words of the future. For example, if a man offers a prize to whoever comes first to the end of a race, the gift is free; and though the words are of the future, the right still passes — for if he had not wanted his words to be so understood, he should not have let the race run.

[Signs Of Contract Are Words Both Of The Past, Present, And Future.] In contracts, the right passes not only where the words are of present or past time, but also where they are of the future. For all contract is mutual transfer, or exchange, of right; and therefore one who promises only because he has already received the benefit for which he promises is to be understood as intending the right to pass. For unless he had been content to have his words so understood, the other party would not have performed his part first. For this reason, in buying and selling and in other contractual acts, a promise is equivalent to a covenant, and therefore binding.

He who performs first in a contract is said to MERIT what he is to receive by the performance of the other; and he has it as due. Likewise when a prize is offered to many, to be given only to the one who wins, or when money is thrown among many to be enjoyed by those who catch it, although this is a free gift, yet so to win or so to catch is to merit, and to have it as DUE. For the right is transferred in the offering of the prize and in the throwing of the money, though it is not determined to whom — that is decided only by the outcome of the contest. But between these two kinds of merit there is this difference: in contract, I merit by virtue of my own power and the contractor's need; in this case of free gift, I am enabled to merit only by the kindness of the giver. In contract, I merit at the contractor's hand that he should part with his right; in this case of gift, I do not merit that the giver should part with his right, but that, once he has parted with it, it should be mine rather than another's. And this I think is the meaning of that distinction in the schools between Meritum Congrui and Meritum Condigni. For God Almighty, having promised paradise to those men (hoodwinked with carnal desires) who can walk through this world according to the precepts and limits prescribed by him, they say that whoever so walks shall merit paradise Ex Congruo. But because no man can demand a right to paradise by his own righteousness or any other power in himself, but only by the free grace of God, they say no man can merit paradise Ex Condigno. This, I say, I think is the meaning of that distinction; but since disputers do not agree on the meaning of their own terms of art any longer than it serves their turn, I will not affirm anything of their meaning. Only this I say: when a gift is given indefinitely, like a prize to be contended for, he who wins merits, and may claim the prize as due.

If a covenant is made in which neither of the parties performs at once, but they trust one another, then in the condition of mere nature (which is a condition of war of every man against every man) it is void upon any reasonable suspicion. But if there is a common power set over them both, with right and force sufficient to compel performance, it is not void. For he who performs first has no assurance that the other will perform afterward, because the bonds of words are too weak to bridle men's ambition, avarice, anger, and other passions, without the fear of some coercive power; and in the condition of mere nature, where all men are equal and judges of the justness of their own fears, no such coercive power can possibly be supposed. And therefore he who performs first only betrays himself to his enemy, contrary to that right (which he can never abandon) of defending his life and his means of living.

But in a civil state, where there is a power set up to constrain those who would otherwise break faith, that fear is no longer reasonable; and for this reason, he who by the covenant is to perform first is obliged to do so.

The cause of fear that makes such a covenant invalid must always be something that arises after the covenant is made — some new fact or other sign of the will not to perform; otherwise it cannot make the covenant void. For what could not hinder a man from promising ought not to be admitted as a hindrance to performing.

He who transfers any right transfers the means of enjoying it, so far as lies in his power. So a man who sells land is understood to transfer the herbage and whatever grows upon it; nor can the seller of a mill turn away the stream that drives it. And those who give a man the right of government in sovereignty are understood to give him the right of levying money to maintain soldiers and of appointing magistrates for the administration of justice.

To make a covenant with brute beasts is impossible, because not understanding our speech they understand nothing of and accept no transfer of right, nor can they transfer any right to another; and without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.

To make a covenant with God is impossible except by the mediation of such people as God speaks to — either by supernatural revelation, or by his lieutenants who govern under him and in his name — for otherwise we do not know whether our covenants are accepted or not. And therefore those who vow anything contrary to any law of nature vow in vain, as being a thing unjust to pay such a vow. And if the thing is commanded by the law of nature, it is not the vow but the law that binds them.

The matter, or subject, of a covenant is always something that falls under deliberation (since to covenant is an act of the will — that is, an act, and the last act, of deliberation), and is therefore always understood to be something to come, and judged possible by the one who covenants to perform.

And therefore, to promise what is known to be impossible is no covenant. But if what was thought possible later proves impossible, the covenant is valid and binds — not to the thing itself, yet to its value; or, if that too is impossible, to the unfeigned endeavor of performing as much as is possible. For no man can be obliged to more.

Men are freed from their covenants in two ways: by performance, or by being forgiven. For performance is the natural end of obligation; and forgiveness is the restoration of liberty, being a retransferring of that right in which the obligation consisted.

Covenants entered into through fear, in the condition of mere nature, are binding. For example, if I covenant to pay a ransom or render service for my life to an enemy, I am bound by it. For it is a contract in which one receives the benefit of life, while the other is to receive money or service for it; and consequently, where no other law (as is the case in mere nature) forbids the performance, the covenant is valid. Therefore prisoners of war, if they are trusted with the payment of their ransom, are obliged to pay it; and if a weaker prince makes a disadvantageous peace with a stronger out of fear, he is bound to keep it — unless (as has been said before) some new and just cause of fear arises to renew the war. And even in commonwealths, if I am forced to redeem myself from a thief by promising him money, I am bound to pay it, until the civil law discharges me. For whatever I may lawfully do without obligation, I may lawfully covenant to do through fear; and what I lawfully covenant, I cannot lawfully break.

An earlier covenant voids a later one. For a man who has passed away his right to one person today does not have it to pass to another tomorrow; and therefore the later promise transfers no right, but is null.

A covenant not to defend myself from force by force is always void. For (as I have shown before) no man can transfer or lay down his right to save himself from death, wounds, and imprisonment — the avoidance of which is the only end of laying down any right. And therefore the promise of not resisting force, in any covenant, transfers no right, nor is binding. For although a man may covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, kill me,” he cannot covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, I will not resist you when you come to kill me.” For man by nature chooses the lesser evil, which is the danger of death in resisting, rather than the greater, which is certain and present death in not resisting. And this is granted to be true by all men, in that they lead criminals to execution and prison with armed men, even though such criminals have consented to the law by which they are condemned.

A covenant to accuse oneself, without assurance of pardon, is likewise invalid. For in the condition of nature, where every man is judge, there is no place for accusation; and in the civil state, accusation is followed by punishment, which being force, a man is not obliged not to resist. The same is also true of the accusation of those by whose condemnation a man falls into misery — such as a father, wife, or benefactor. For the testimony of such an accuser, if it is not willingly given, is presumed to be corrupted by nature, and therefore not to be received; and where a man's testimony is not to be credited, he is not bound to give it. Likewise, accusations under torture are not to be reckoned as testimony. For torture is to be used only as a means of guesswork and light in the further examination and search for truth; and what is confessed under it tends to the relief of the one being tortured, not to the informing of the torturers. It therefore ought not to have the credit of sufficient testimony — for whether he delivers himself by true accusation or false, he does so by the right of preserving his own life.

Since the force of words (as I have noted before) is too weak to hold men to the performance of their covenants, there are in man's nature only two imaginable helps to strengthen it. These are either a fear of the consequences of breaking one's word, or a glory or pride in appearing not to need to break it. The latter is a generosity too rarely found to be relied on, especially in the pursuers of wealth, command, or sensual pleasure, who make up the greatest part of mankind. The passion to be reckoned upon is fear; of which there are two very general objects: one, the power of spirits invisible; the other, the power of those men one will offend by breaking faith. Of these two, though the former is the greater power, the fear of the latter is commonly the greater fear. The fear of the former is in every man his own religion, which has its place in the nature of man before civil society. The latter does not — at least not enough place to keep men to their promises, because in the condition of mere nature the inequality of power is not perceived but by the outcome of battle. So before the time of civil society, or in its interruption by war, there is nothing that can strengthen a covenant of peace agreed upon against the temptations of avarice, ambition, lust, or other strong desire, but the fear of that invisible power which each one worships as God, and fears as an avenger of their treachery. All therefore that can be done between two men not subject to civil power is to put one another to swear by the God he fears. This swearing, or OATH, is a form of speech, added to a promise, by which the one who promises signifies that, unless he performs, he renounces the mercy of his God, or calls upon him for vengeance on himself. Such was the heathen form: “Let Jupiter kill me else, as I kill this Beast.” So is our form: “I shall do thus, and thus, so help me God.” And this, with the rites and ceremonies each one uses in his own religion, so that the fear of breaking faith might be the greater.

From this it appears that an oath taken according to any form or rite other than that of the one who swears is in vain, and no oath. And there is no swearing by anything that the swearer does not think is God. For although men have sometimes used to swear by their kings, out of fear or flattery, they would thereby have it understood that they attributed divine honor to them. And swearing unnecessarily by God is just profaning his name; and swearing by other things, as men do in common talk, is not swearing but an impious custom, picked up from too much vehemence in talking.

It also appears that the oath adds nothing to the obligation. For a covenant, if lawful, binds in the sight of God without the oath as much as with it; if unlawful, it does not bind at all, even though confirmed by an oath.

chapters.title: Chapter XV. Of Other Lawes of Nature
paragraphs: From that law of nature by which we are obliged to transfer to another such rights as, being retained, hinder the peace of mankind, there follows a third: That men perform their covenants made. Without this, covenants are in vain and empty words; and the right of all men to all things still remaining, we are still in the condition of war.

And in this law of nature consists the fountain and origin of JUSTICE. For where no covenant has preceded, no right has been transferred, and every man has a right to everything; consequently, no action can be unjust. But when a covenant is made, then to break it is unjust. And the definition of INJUSTICE is no other than the not-performance of covenant. Whatever is not unjust is just.

[Justice And Property Begin With The Constitution Of Commonwealth.] But because covenants of mutual trust, where there is a fear of non-performance on either side (as was said in the previous chapter), are invalid, then although the origin of justice is the making of covenants, yet there can actually be no injustice until the cause of such fear is taken away — which, while men are in the natural condition of war, cannot be done. Therefore, before the names of just and unjust can have a place, there must be some coercive power to compel men equally to the performance of their covenants, by the terror of some punishment greater than the benefit they expect from breaking the covenant; and to make good that property which by mutual contract men acquire in recompense of the universal right they abandon. And no such power exists before the establishment of a commonwealth. This may also be gathered from the ordinary definition of justice in the schools: for they say that “Justice is the constant Will of giving to every man his own.” And therefore, where there is no “own” — that is, no property — there is no injustice; and where no coercive power has been set up — that is, where there is no commonwealth — there is no property, all men having a right to all things. Therefore, where there is no commonwealth, nothing is unjust. So the nature of justice consists in keeping valid covenants; but the validity of covenants does not begin until the establishment of a civil power sufficient to compel men to keep them. It is then also that property begins.

The fool has said in his heart that there is no such thing as justice — and sometimes also out loud — seriously claiming that since every man's preservation and contentment is committed to his own care, there could be no reason why every man should not do whatever he thinks conduces to it, and therefore that to make or not make, keep or not keep covenants is not against reason when it conduces to one's own benefit. He does not in this deny that there are covenants, that they are sometimes broken and sometimes kept, and that such breach may be called injustice and the observance of them justice. But he asks whether injustice, taking away the fear of God (for the same fool has said in his heart there is no God), may not sometimes stand with that reason which dictates to every man his own good — particularly when it conduces to such a benefit as will put a man in a condition to disregard not only the disapproval and reviling of others but also their power. The kingdom of God is taken by violence — but what if it could be taken by unjust violence? Would it be against reason so to take it, when it is impossible to be hurt by doing so? And if it is not against reason, it is not against justice; otherwise justice is not to be approved as good. From reasoning of this sort, successful wickedness has gotten the name of virtue; and some who in all other things have disallowed the violation of faith have allowed it when it is for the gaining of a kingdom. And the heathen who believed that Saturn was deposed by his son Jupiter still believed the same Jupiter to be the avenger of injustice — somewhat like a piece of law in Coke's Commentaries on Littleton, where he says that if the rightful heir to the crown is attainted of treason, yet the crown shall descend to him, and Eo Instante (at that very instant) the attainder is void. From such examples a man would be very ready to infer that when the heir apparent of a kingdom kills the one in possession — even his own father — you may call it injustice, or by whatever name you like, but it can never be against reason, since all voluntary actions of men aim at their own benefit, and those actions are most reasonable which most conduce to their ends. This specious reasoning is nevertheless false.

For the question is not about mutual promises where there is no security of performance on either side (as when no civil power has been erected over the promising parties — for such promises are no covenants); but either where one of the parties has already performed, or where there is a power to make him perform. There the question is whether it is against reason — that is, against the benefit of the other party — to perform or not. And I say it is not against reason. To make this clear, we should consider: first, when a man does something that, despite anything that can be foreseen and reckoned upon, tends to his own destruction, yet some accident he could not have expected may turn it to his benefit, such events do not make the action reasonably or wisely done. Second, in a condition of war, in which every man, for lack of a common power to keep them all in awe, is an enemy to every other man, no one can hope by his own strength or wit to defend himself from destruction without the help of confederates. Each one in the confederation expects the same defense from it that any other does. Therefore, anyone who declares that he thinks it reasonable to deceive those who help him can reasonably expect no other means of safety than what can be had from his own single power. He, then, who breaks his covenant — and consequently declares that he thinks he may with reason do so — cannot be received into any society united for peace and defense, except by the mistake of those who receive him; nor, when he has been received, can he be kept in it without their seeing the danger of their mistake. And a man cannot reasonably reckon upon such mistakes by others as the means of his security. Therefore, if he is left out of or cast out of society, he perishes; and if he lives in society, it is by the errors of other men, which he could not foresee or reckon upon, and consequently against the reason of his preservation. So all men who do not contribute to his destruction forbear him only out of ignorance of what is good for themselves.

As for the example of gaining the secure and perpetual happiness of heaven by any means — that is frivolous, since there is only one way imaginable, and that is not breaking, but keeping, of covenant.

And as for the other example, of attaining sovereignty by rebellion — it is plain that even if the outcome follows, it cannot reasonably be expected, but rather the contrary; and because by gaining it this way, others are taught to gain the same in the like manner, the attempt is against reason. Justice therefore — that is, keeping of covenant — is a rule of reason by which we are forbidden to do anything destructive of our life; and consequently a law of nature.

Some go further and would have the law of nature be not those rules which conduce to the preservation of man's life on earth, but to the attaining of an eternal happiness after death — to which they think the breach of covenant may conduce, and consequently be just and reasonable. (Such are those who think it a work of merit to kill, depose, or rebel against the sovereign power constituted over them by their own consent.) But since there is no natural knowledge of man's condition after death, much less of the reward then to be given to breach of faith — only a belief grounded on what other men say, that they know it supernaturally, or that they know those who knew them, who knew others, who knew it supernaturally — breach of faith cannot be called a precept of reason or nature.

Others, who allow the keeping of faith to be a law of nature, nevertheless make exceptions of certain persons — such as heretics and those who do not perform their covenants to others. This too is against reason. For if any fault of a man is enough to discharge our covenant once made, the same ought in reason to have been enough to have prevented its being made in the first place.

The names just and unjust, when applied to men, mean one thing; when applied to actions, another. Applied to men, they signify the conformity or non-conformity of their manners to reason. Applied to actions, they signify the conformity or non-conformity to reason, not of manners or way of life, but of particular actions. A just man, therefore, is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just; and an unjust man is one who neglects this. In our language such men are more often called righteous and unrighteous than just and unjust, though the meaning is the same. So a righteous man does not lose that title for one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistake about things or persons; nor does an unrighteous man lose his character for the actions he does, or refrains from doing, out of fear — because his will is not formed by justice but by the apparent benefit of what he is to do. What gives human actions the relish of justice is a certain nobleness or gallantry of courage (rarely found) by which a man scorns to be indebted for the contentment of his life to fraud or breach of promise. This justice of the manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue, and injustice a vice.
But the justice of actions denominates men not just but guiltless; and the injustice of the same (also called injury) gives them only the name of guilty.

Again, the injustice of manners is the disposition or aptitude to do injury; and is injustice before it proceeds to act, and without supposing any individual person injured. But the injustice of an action (that is to say, injury) supposes an individual person injured — namely, the one to whom the covenant was made. So many times the injury is received by one man while the damage falls upon another. As when the master commands his servant to give money to a stranger; if it is not done, the injury is done to the master, whom the servant had previously covenanted to obey; but the damage falls on the stranger, to whom the servant had no obligation, and therefore could not injure. And likewise in commonwealths, private men may forgive one another their debts, but not robberies or other violences by which they are damaged. For the withholding of a debt is an injury to themselves; but robbery and violence are injuries to the person of the commonwealth.

Whatever is done to a man in conformity with his own will signified to the doer is no injury to him. For if the one who does it has not by some prior covenant passed away his original right to do what he pleases, there is no breach of covenant, and therefore no injury done him. And if he has, then his will to have it done, being signified, is a release of that covenant — and so again there is no injury done him.

Justice of actions is divided by writers into Commutative and Distributive; the former, they say, consists in arithmetical proportion, the latter in geometrical proportion. Commutative justice, they place in the equality of value of the things contracted for; distributive, in the distribution of equal benefit to men of equal merit. As if it were injustice to sell dearer than we buy, or to give more to a man than he deserves. But the value of all things contracted for is measured by the appetite of the contractors, and therefore the just value is what they are content to give. And merit (besides the merit that is by covenant — where performance on one part merits performance of the other, and which falls under commutative, not distributive, justice) is not due as a matter of justice; it is rewarded only as a matter of grace. Therefore this distinction, in the sense in which it is usually expounded, is not right. To speak properly, commutative justice is the justice of a contractor — that is, performance of covenant in buying and selling, hiring and letting to hire, lending and borrowing, exchanging, bartering, and other acts of contract.

And distributive justice is the justice of an arbitrator — that is, the act of defining what is just. In doing this, being trusted by those who make him arbitrator, if he performs his trust he is said to distribute to every man his own. And this is indeed just distribution, and may be called (though improperly) distributive justice; but more properly it is equity, which is also a law of nature, as shall be shown in due place.

As justice depends on antecedent covenant, so gratitude depends on antecedent grace — that is, on antecedent free gift. And this is the fourth law of nature, which may be put in this form: “That a man which receiveth Benefit from another of meer Grace, Endeavour that he which giveth it, have no reasonable cause to repent him of his good will.” For no man gives except with intention of good to himself, because gift is voluntary, and of all voluntary acts the object is, to every man, his own good. If men see they will be frustrated of this, there will be no beginning of benevolence or trust, nor consequently of mutual help, nor of reconciliation of one man to another; and therefore they must remain in the condition of war, which is contrary to the first and fundamental law of nature, which commands men to seek peace. The breach of this law is called ingratitude; and it has the same relation to grace that injustice has to obligation by covenant.

A fifth law of nature is COMPLAISANCE — that is, “That every man strive to accommodate himselfe to the rest.” To understand this, we may consider that in men's aptness for society there is a diversity of nature, arising from their diversity of affections, not unlike what we see in stones brought together for the building of an edifice. As that stone which by the roughness and irregularity of its shape takes more room from others than it itself fills, and because of its hardness cannot easily be made flat — and so hinders the building — is by the builders cast away as unprofitable and troublesome, so a man who by roughness of nature will strive to retain those things which to himself are superfluous and to others necessary, and because of the stubbornness of his passions cannot be corrected, is to be left out or cast out of society as a burden to it. For seeing that every man, not only by right but also by necessity of nature, is presumed to endeavor all he can to obtain what is necessary for his preservation, anyone who opposes him in this for the sake of superfluous things is guilty of the war that follows from it, and therefore does what is contrary to the fundamental law of nature, which commands him to seek peace. The observers of this law may be called SOCIABLE (the Latins call them Commodi); the contrary, stubborn, unsociable, peevish, intractable.

A sixth law of nature is this: “That upon caution of the Future time, a man ought to pardon the offences past of them that repenting, desire it.” For pardon is nothing but the granting of peace; which, though granted to those who persist in their hostility is not peace but fear, yet not granted to those who give caution for future time is a sign of an aversion to peace, and therefore contrary to the law of nature.
[The Seventh: That In Revenges, Men Respect Only The Future Good.]

A seventh is: “That in Revenges, (that is, retribution of evil for evil,) Men look not at the greatnesse of the evill past, but the greatnesse of the good to follow.” By this we are forbidden to inflict punishment with any other design than for the correction of the offender or the direction of others. For this law follows from the previous one, which commands pardon upon security of the future time. Besides, revenge without regard to the example and the good to come is a triumph or glorying in another's hurt, tending to no end (for the end is always something to come); and glorying to no end is vainglory, and contrary to reason. To hurt without reason tends to the bringing-in of war, which is against the law of nature; and is commonly called by the name of cruelty.

And because all signs of hatred or contempt provoke fighting — to the point that most men would rather hazard their life than not be avenged — we may, in the eighth place, lay down this precept as a law of nature: “That no man by deed, word, countenance, or gesture, declare Hatred, or Contempt of another.” The breach of this law is commonly called contumely.

The question of who is the better man has no place in the condition of mere nature, where (as has been shown before) all men are equal. The inequality that now exists has been introduced by the civil laws. I know that Aristotle, in the first book of his Politics, as a foundation of his doctrine, makes men by nature — some more worthy to command, meaning the wiser sort (such as he thought himself to be on account of his philosophy), and others to serve (meaning those who had strong bodies but were not philosophers as he was) — as if master and servant were introduced not by the consent of men but by difference of wit. This is not only against reason but also against experience. For there are very few so foolish that they would not rather govern themselves than be governed by others; nor, when those who are wise in their own conceit contend by force with those who distrust their own wisdom, do they always — or often, or hardly ever — get the victory. If, then, nature has made men equal, that equality is to be acknowledged; or if nature has made men unequal, yet, because men who think themselves equal will not enter into conditions of peace except on equal terms, such equality must be admitted. And therefore, as the ninth law of nature, I lay down this: “That every man acknowledge other for his Equall by Nature.” The breach of this precept is pride.

On this law depends another: “That at the entrance into conditions of Peace, no man require to reserve to himselfe any Right, which he is not content should be reserved to every one of the rest.” As it is necessary for all who seek peace to lay down certain rights of nature — that is, not to have the liberty to do everything they please — so it is necessary for man's life to retain some, such as the right to govern their own bodies, to enjoy air, water, motion, and the means of going from place to place, and all other things without which a man cannot live, or cannot live well. If, in this case, at the making of peace, men require for themselves what they would not have granted to others, they act contrary to the previous law that commands the acknowledgment of natural equality, and therefore also against the law of nature. The observers of this law are those we call modest, and its breakers, arrogant men. The Greeks call the violation of this law pleonexia (πλεονεξία) — that is, a desire of more than one's share.

Also, “If a man be trusted to judge between man and man,” it is a precept of the law of nature, “that he deale Equally between them.” For without that, the controversies of men cannot be settled except by war. He who is partial in judgment does what lies in his power to deter men from the use of judges and arbitrators, and consequently (against the fundamental law of nature) is a cause of war.

The observance of this law — by the equal distribution to each man of what in reason belongs to him — is called EQUITY, and (as I have said before) distributive justice. Its violation is called acceptance of persons, Prosopolepsia (προσωποληψία).

And from this follows another law: “That such things as cannot be divided, be enjoyed in Common, if it can be; and if the quantity of the thing permit, without Stint; otherwise Proportionably to the number of them that have Right.” For otherwise the distribution is unequal, and contrary to equity.

But there are some things that can neither be divided nor enjoyed in common. Then the law of nature, which prescribes equity, requires: “That the Entire Right; or else, (making the use alternate,) the First Possession, be determined by Lot.” For equal distribution is of the law of nature, and no other means of equal distribution can be imagined.

Of lots there are two sorts: arbitrary and natural. Arbitrary, when agreed on by the competitors. Natural, either primogeniture (which the Greek calls Kleronomia (κληρονομία), meaning “given by lot”) or first seizure.
And therefore those things which cannot be enjoyed in common, nor divided, ought to be adjudged to the first possessor; and in some cases to the firstborn, as acquired by lot.

It is also a law of nature: “That all men that mediate Peace, be allowed safe Conduct.” For the law that commands peace as the end commands intercession as the means, and to intercession the means is safe conduct.

And because, however willing men may be to observe these laws, questions may nevertheless arise about a man's action: first, whether it was done or not; second (if done), whether against the law or not against it — the former being called a question of fact, the latter a question of right. Therefore, unless the parties to the question covenant mutually to stand by the verdict of another, they are as far from peace as ever. This other, to whose verdict they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And therefore it is of the law of nature: “That they that are at controversie, submit their Right to the judgement of an Arbitrator.”

And since every man is presumed to do all things with a view to his own benefit, no man is a fit arbitrator in his own cause. And if he were ever so fit, yet, equity allowing equal benefit to each party, if one is admitted to be judge, the other must be admitted also; and so the controversy — that is, the cause of war — remains, against the law of nature.
[The Eighteenth: No Man To Be Judge, That Has In Him Cause Of Partiality.]

For the same reason no man in any cause ought to be accepted as arbitrator to whom greater profit, or honor, or pleasure plainly arises from the victory of one party than from the other. For he has taken (though an unavoidable bribe, yet) a bribe; and no man can be obliged to trust him. And so the controversy and the condition of war remain, contrary to the law of nature.

And in a controversy of fact, the judge, having no more credit to give to one than to the other (if there are no other arguments), must give credit to a third, or to a third and a fourth, or to more. Otherwise the question is undecided, and left to force, contrary to the law of nature.

These are the laws of nature, dictating peace as a means of the preservation of men in multitudes, and which alone concern the doctrine of civil society. There are other things tending to the destruction of particular men, such as drunkenness and all other parts of intemperance, which may therefore also be reckoned among those things that the law of nature has forbidden; but they are not necessary to mention and not pertinent enough to this place.

And although this may seem too subtle a deduction of the laws of nature to be noticed by all men — most of whom are too busy getting food, and the rest too negligent to understand — yet, to leave all men without excuse, the laws of nature have been summed up into one easy formula, intelligible even to the meanest capacity: “Do not that to another, which thou wouldest not have done to thy selfe.” This shows him that he has no more to do, in learning the laws of nature, than, when weighing the actions of other men against his own, they seem too heavy, to put them into the other side of the balance and his own into their place, so that his own passions and self-love may add nothing to the weight; and then there is none of these laws of nature that will not seem to him very reasonable.

[But In Effect Then Only When There Is Security.] The laws of nature oblige In Foro Interno (in the inward forum, that is, in conscience) — that is, they bind to a desire that they should take place; but In Foro Externo (in the outward forum, that is, in public action) — that is, to putting them into practice — not always. For a man who should be modest and tractable and perform all he promises in such a time and place where no one else does the same would only make himself a prey to others, and procure his own certain ruin, contrary to the ground of all the laws of nature, which is the preservation of nature. And again, he who observes the same laws toward one who does not observe them himself does not seek peace but war, and consequently the destruction of his own nature by violence.

And whatever laws bind in foro interno may be broken not only by an act contrary to the law, but also by an act according to it, in case a man thinks it contrary. For although his action in this case is according to the law, yet his purpose, where the obligation is in foro interno, is a breach.

The laws of nature are immutable and eternal. For injustice, ingratitude, arrogance, pride, iniquity, acceptance of persons, and the rest can never be made lawful. For it can never be that war shall preserve life and peace destroy it.

The same laws, because they oblige only to a desire and endeavor — I mean an unfeigned and constant endeavor — are easy to observe. For in that they require nothing but endeavor, anyone who endeavors their performance fulfills them; and whoever fulfills the law is just.

And the science of them is the true and only moral philosophy. For moral philosophy is nothing else but the science of what is good and evil in the conversation and society of mankind. Good and evil are names that signify our appetites and aversions, which in different tempers, customs, and doctrines of men are different. Different men differ not only in their judgment of what is pleasant or unpleasant to the taste, smell, hearing, touch, and sight, but also of what is in conformity with, or contrary to, reason in the actions of common life. Indeed, the same man at different times differs from himself, and at one time praises — that is, calls good — what at another time he dispraises and calls evil. From this arise disputes, controversies, and at last war. And therefore, so long as a man is in the condition of mere nature (which is a condition of war), private appetite is the measure of good and evil. Consequently, all men agree on this: that peace is good, and therefore also the way or means of peace — which (as I have shown before) are justice, gratitude, modesty, equity, mercy, and the rest of the laws of nature — are good; that is to say, moral virtues. And their contrary, vices, are evil. Now the science of virtue and vice is moral philosophy, and therefore the true doctrine of the laws of nature is the true moral philosophy. But the writers of moral philosophy, though they acknowledge the same virtues and vices, yet not seeing wherein their goodness consisted, nor that they come to be praised as the means of peaceful, sociable, and comfortable living, place them in a mediocrity of passions — as if not the cause, but the degree of daring, made fortitude; or not the cause, but the quantity, of a gift made liberality.

These dictates of reason men usually call by the name of laws, but improperly. For they are only conclusions, or theorems, concerning what conduces to the preservation and defense of themselves; whereas a law, properly, is the word of him who by right has command over others. Yet if we consider the same theorems as delivered in the word of God, who by right commands all things, then they are properly called laws.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI. Of Persons, Authors, and Things Personated
paragraphs: A PERSON is one “whose words or actions are considered, either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of an other man, or of any other thing to whom they are attributed, whether Truly or by Fiction.”
When they are considered as his own, he is called a natural person. And when they are considered as representing the words and actions of another, he is a feigned or artificial person.

The word Person is Latin; instead of which the Greeks have Prosopon (πρόσωπον), meaning “the face,” just as Persona in Latin means the disguise or outward appearance of a man, counterfeited on the stage — and sometimes more particularly that part of it which disguises the face, like a mask or visor. From the stage it has been transferred to any representer of speech and action, in tribunals as well as in theaters. So a person is the same thing as an actor, both on the stage and in ordinary conversation; and to personate is to act, or represent, oneself or another. He who acts another is said to bear his person, or to act in his name (in which sense Cicero uses it when he says, “Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis,” “I bear three persons: my own, my adversary's, and the judge's”). In various contexts he is called variously: a representer, or representative, a lieutenant, a vicar, an attorney, a deputy, a procurator, an actor, and the like.

Of artificial persons, some have their words and actions owned by those whom they represent. Then the person is the actor, and he who owns his words and actions is the AUTHOR; in which case the actor acts by authority. For what is called an owner in speaking of goods and possessions (in Latin Dominus, in Greek Kurios (κύριος)), in speaking of actions is called Author. And as the right of possession is called Dominion, so the right of doing any action is called AUTHORITY. So by authority is always understood a right of doing any act; and Done By Authority means done by commission, or license from him whose right it is.

From this it follows that when an actor makes a covenant by authority, he thereby binds the author no less than if he had made it himself; and no less subjects him to all the consequences of it. And therefore all that has been said before (in Chapter 14) of the nature of covenants between man and man in their natural capacity is also true when those covenants are made by their actors, representers, or procurators who have authority from them — so far as is within their commission, but no further.

And therefore he who makes a covenant with the actor or representer without knowing the authority he has does so at his own peril. For no man is bound by a covenant of which he is not the author; nor consequently by a covenant made against, or beyond, the authority he gave.

When the actor does anything against the law of nature by the command of the author, if he is bound by an earlier covenant to obey him, then it is not the actor but the author who breaks the law of nature. For though the action is against the law of nature, it is not his; on the contrary, to refuse to do it is against the law of nature, which forbids breach of covenant.

And he who makes a covenant with the author by the mediation of the actor, not knowing what authority he has but only taking his word, is no longer bound if such authority is not made evident to him upon demand. For the covenant made with the author is not valid without his counter-assurance.
