But if the one who so covenants knew beforehand that he was to expect no other assurance than the actor's word, then the covenant is valid, because the actor in this case makes himself the author. And therefore, just as when the authority is evident the covenant binds the author and not the actor, so when the authority is feigned it binds only the actor; there being no author but himself.

There are few things that are incapable of being represented by fiction. Inanimate things, such as a church, a hospital, a bridge, may be personated by a rector, master, or overseer. But inanimate things cannot be authors, and therefore cannot give authority to their actors. Yet the actors may have authority — given them by those who are owners or governors of those things — to procure their maintenance. And therefore such things cannot be personated before there is some state of civil government.

Likewise children, fools, and madmen who have no use of reason may be personated by guardians or curators; but they cannot be authors (during that time) of any action done by them, any longer than (when they recover the use of reason) they shall judge it reasonable. Yet during the folly, he who has the right of governing them may give authority to the guardian. But this again has no place except in a civil state, because before such a state there is no dominion of persons.

An idol, or mere figment of the brain, may be personated, as the gods of the heathen were — personated by such officers as the state appointed, and holding possessions and other goods and rights which men from time to time dedicated and consecrated to them. But idols cannot be authors, for an idol is nothing. The authority proceeded from the state, and therefore before the introduction of civil government the gods of the heathen could not be personated.

The true God may be personated. As he was, first, by Moses — who governed the Israelites (who were not his, but God's people) not in his own name, with Hoc Dicit Moses (“Moses says this”), but in God's name, with Hoc Dicit Dominus (“The Lord says this”). Second, by the Son of Man — his own Son, our Blessed Saviour Jesus Christ, who came to reduce the Jews and induct all nations into the kingdom of his Father, not from himself but as sent from his Father. And third, by the Holy Ghost, or Comforter, speaking and working in the apostles — which Holy Ghost was a Comforter that came not from himself but was sent, and proceeded from them both.

A multitude of men is made one person when they are represented by one man, or one person, provided this is done with the consent of every one of that multitude in particular. For it is the unity of the representer, not the unity of the represented, that makes the person one. And it is the representer who bears the person, and only one person; and unity cannot otherwise be understood in a multitude.

And because the multitude is naturally not one, but many, they cannot be understood as one but as many authors, of everything their representative says or does in their name. Every man gives the common representer authority from himself in particular, and owns all the actions the representer does, in case they give him authority without limit. Otherwise, when they limit him in what and how far he shall represent them, none of them owns more than they gave him commission to act.

And if the representative consists of many men, the voice of the greater number must be considered as the voice of them all. For if the smaller number pronounce, for example, in the affirmative, and the greater in the negative, there will be negatives more than enough to destroy the affirmatives; and so the excess of negatives, standing uncontradicted, are the only voice the representative has.

And a representative of even number — especially when the number is not great — by which the contradictory voices are often equal, is therefore often mute and incapable of action. Yet in some cases contradictory voices equal in number may determine a question; as in condemning or absolving, equality of votes — even by not condemning — absolves; but the reverse is not true, that not absolving condemns. For when a cause is heard, not to condemn is to absolve; but to say that not absolving is condemning is not true. The like holds in a deliberation about executing immediately or deferring to another time: when the voices are equal, not decreeing execution is a decree of delay.

Or if the number is odd — three or more (men, or assemblies) — of whom every one has by a negative voice the authority to take away the effect of all the affirmative voices of the rest, this number is no representative. For by the diversity of opinions and interests of men it often becomes, and in cases of the greatest consequence, a mute person — unfit, as for many other things, so for the government of a multitude, especially in time of war.

Of authors there are two sorts. The first, simply so called — whom I have before defined as one who simply owns the action of another. The second is one who owns an action, or covenant, of another conditionally — that is, who undertakes to do it if the other does not do it at, or before, a certain time. These conditional authors are generally called SURETIES, in Latin Fidejussores and Sponsores; and particularly, for debt, Praedes; and for appearance before a judge or magistrate, Vades.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII. Of the Causes, Generation, and Definition of a Common-wealth
paragraphs: The final cause, end, or design of men (who naturally love liberty and dominion over others) in laying upon themselves the restraint in which we see them live in commonwealths is the foresight of their own preservation, and of a more contented life thereby — that is, of getting themselves out of the miserable condition of war which is the necessary consequence (as has been shown) of the natural passions of men when there is no visible power to keep them in awe, and to bind them, by fear of punishment, to the performance of their covenants and the observance of those laws of nature set down in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

For the laws of nature — justice, equity, modesty, mercy, and (in short) doing to others as we would be done by — are by themselves, without the terror of some power to enforce them, contrary to our natural passions, which carry us to partiality, pride, revenge, and the like. And covenants without the sword are only words, with no strength to secure a man at all. So, in spite of the laws of nature (which each man keeps when he has the will to keep them and can do so safely), if there is no power erected, or none great enough for our security, every man will and may lawfully rely on his own strength and skill as his guard against all other men. In all places where men have lived in small families, robbing and despoiling one another has been a trade, and so far from being reckoned as contrary to the law of nature, the greater the spoils gained, the greater the honour. The only laws they observed in this were the laws of honour: to abstain from cruelty, to leave men their lives and the instruments of farming. And as small families did then, so cities and kingdoms — which are only larger families — do now. For their own security they enlarge their dominions, using as pretexts every danger and every fear of invasion, or of aid that might be given to invaders, and try as far as they can to subdue or weaken their neighbours, by open force and by secret arts, for want of any other guarantee — and they consider this just, and are remembered for it in later ages with honour.

Nor is it the mere joining together of a small number of men that gives them this security. In small numbers, a small addition on one side or the other makes such a great difference in strength that it is enough to decide the victory, and so gives encouragement to an invasion. The multitude sufficient to rely on for our security is not fixed at any specific number, but is decided by comparison with the enemy we fear; and it is sufficient when the enemy's advantage is not so visibly and conspicuously decisive of the outcome of a war as to move him to attempt one.

And let the multitude be ever so great: if their actions are directed by their individual judgements and individual appetites, they can expect from that no defence nor protection — neither against a common enemy nor against the injuries of one another. For being divided in opinion about the best use of their strength, they do not help but hinder each other, and reduce their strength by mutual opposition to nothing. By this they are easily not only subdued by a very few who agree together, but, when there is no common enemy, they make war on each other for their particular interests. For if we could suppose a great multitude of men to agree in observing justice and the other laws of nature without a common power to keep them all in awe, we might as well suppose all mankind to do the same; and then there neither would be, nor would there need to be, any civil government or commonwealth at all, because there would be peace without subjection.

Nor is it enough, for the security that men want to last all their life long, to be governed and directed by one judgement for a limited time — as in one battle, or one war. For though they win a victory by their united effort against a foreign enemy, yet afterwards, when either they have no common enemy, or the one that one side counts as an enemy is counted as a friend by another, they must inevitably, through their different interests, dissolve and fall back into war among themselves.

It is true that certain living creatures — bees and ants — live sociably with one another (which is why Aristotle numbers them among the political creatures); and yet they have no other direction than their individual judgements and appetites, nor any speech by which one of them can communicate to another what it thinks expedient for the common benefit. So one might want to know why mankind cannot do the same. To this I answer:

First, that men are continually in competition for honour and dignity, which these creatures are not; and so among men there arises on that ground envy and hatred, and finally war — but among these creatures, no such thing.

Second, that among these creatures the common good does not differ from the private good; and being inclined by nature to their private good, they thereby procure the common benefit. But man, whose joy consists in comparing himself with other men, can relish nothing that is not eminent.

Third, that these creatures, not having (as man does) the use of reason, do not see, or think they see, any fault in the administration of their common business. Whereas among men there are many who think themselves wiser, and better able to govern the public, than the rest; and these strive to reform and innovate, one in this direction, another in that, and thereby bring it into discord and civil war.

Fourth, that these creatures, though they have some use of voice in making known to one another their desires and other affections, lack the art of words, by which some men can represent to others good in the likeness of evil, and evil in the likeness of good, and magnify or diminish the apparent size of good and evil — making men discontented and disturbing their peace at will.

Fifth, irrational creatures cannot distinguish between injury and damage; and so, so long as they are at ease, they are not offended with their fellows. Man, on the other hand, is most troublesome when he is most at ease: for then is when he loves to show off his wisdom and to find fault with the actions of those who govern the commonwealth.

Last, the agreement of these creatures is natural; that of men is by covenant only, which is artificial. So it is no wonder that something more (besides covenant) is needed to make their agreement constant and lasting — namely, a common power, to keep them in awe and to direct their actions to the common benefit.

The only way to erect such a common power as may be able to defend them from the invasion of foreigners and from the injuries done by one to another — and so to secure them in such a way that by their own industry and by the fruits of the earth they may feed themselves and live contentedly — is to transfer all their power and strength upon one man, or upon one assembly of men, that may reduce all their wills, by plurality of votes, to one will. This is the same as appointing one man, or one assembly of men, to bear their person; and every one to own and acknowledge himself the author of whatever the bearer of their person shall do, or cause to be done, in those things that concern the common peace and safety — and to that end to submit each one's will to his will, and each one's judgement to his judgement. This is more than consent, or concord: it is a real unity of them all in one and the same person, made by covenant of every man with every man, in such a way that it is as if every man should say to every man, 'I authorise, and give up, my right of governing myself, to this man, or to this assembly of men, on this condition: that you give up your right to him, and authorise all his actions in like manner.' This done, the multitude so united in one person is called a COMMONWEALTH — in Latin, CIVITAS. This is the generation of that great LEVIATHAN, or rather (to speak more reverently) of that mortal god, to which, under the immortal God, we owe our peace and defence. For by this authority, given to him by every particular man in the commonwealth, he has the use of so much power and strength conferred on him that, by the terror of it, he is enabled to mould the wills of them all to peace at home and to mutual aid against their enemies abroad.

And in him consists the essence of the commonwealth — which (to define it) is: one person, of whose acts a great multitude, by mutual covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the author, to the end that he may use the strength and means of them all as he shall think expedient for their peace and common defence.
And the one who bears this person is called the SOVEREIGN, and is said to have sovereign power; and every other man is his SUBJECT.

There are two ways of attaining this sovereign power. One is by natural force — as when a man compels his children to submit themselves and their children to his government, being able to destroy them if they refuse; or when by war he subdues his enemies to his will, sparing their lives on that condition. The other is when men agree among themselves to submit voluntarily to some man, or some assembly of men, trusting that they will be protected by him against all others. The latter may be called a political commonwealth, or commonwealth by institution; the former, a commonwealth by acquisition. I shall speak first of the commonwealth by institution.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII. Of the Rights of Soveraignes by Institution
paragraphs: A commonwealth is said to be instituted when a multitude of men agree, and covenant, every one with every one, that whatever man, or assembly of men, shall be given by the majority the right to present the person of them all (that is, to be their representative), every one — both those who voted for him and those who voted against him — shall authorise all the actions and judgements of that man, or assembly of men, as if they were his own; and that this is done to the end of living peaceably among themselves and being protected against other men.
From this institution of a commonwealth are derived all the rights and faculties of the man, or men, on whom sovereign power is conferred by the consent of the people assembled.

First, because they covenant, it is to be understood that they are not bound by any prior covenant to anything contrary to this. Consequently, those who have already instituted a commonwealth, being bound by covenant to own the actions and judgements of one man, cannot lawfully make a new covenant among themselves to be obedient to any other in any matter without his permission. And so the subjects of a monarch cannot, without his leave, cast off monarchy and return to the confusion of a disunited multitude; nor transfer the person of him who bears it to another man, or to another assembly of men. For they are bound, every man to every man, to own and be reputed the author of all that he who is already their sovereign shall do and judge fit to be done; so that if any one man dissents, all the rest would break their covenant made with that man, which is injustice. They have also each given the sovereignty to the one who bears their person; so if they depose him, they take from him what is his own — which is again injustice. Besides, if the man who attempts to depose his sovereign is killed, or punished by him for the attempt, he is the author of his own punishment, being by the institution the author of all his sovereign does. And since it is unjust for a man to do anything for which he may be punished by his own authority, he is also, on that count, unjust. As for those who have pretended, as ground for disobedience to their sovereign, a new covenant made not with men but with God — that too is unjust. There is no covenant with God except through the mediation of some person who represents God's person; and none does that but God's lieutenant, who holds sovereignty under God. But this pretence of covenant with God is so plain a lie, even in the consciences of those who claim it, that it is an act not only of an unjust but also of a vile and unmanly disposition.

Second, because the right of bearing the person of them all is given to the man they make sovereign by covenant only of one to another, and not of him to any of them, no breach of covenant on the part of the sovereign can occur; and consequently none of his subjects, by any pretence of forfeiture, can be freed from his subjection. That the one made sovereign makes no covenant with his subjects beforehand is clear: for he must make it either with the whole multitude as one party to the covenant, or he must make a separate covenant with each man. With the whole, as one party, is impossible: as yet they are not one person. And if he makes as many separate covenants as there are men, then those covenants, after he has the sovereignty, are void; because whatever act any one of them may claim as a breach of it is the act both of himself and of every other, being done in the person of each, and by the right of every one of them in particular. Besides, if any one or more of them allege a breach of a covenant made by the sovereign at his institution, and others — or one other subject, or the sovereign himself alone — deny that any such breach took place, there is in that case no judge to decide the controversy; it returns therefore to the sword, and every man recovers the right of protecting himself by his own strength — contrary to the design they had in the institution. It is therefore pointless to grant sovereignty by way of any prior covenant. The opinion that any monarch receives his power by covenant — that is, on conditions — comes from a failure to grasp this easy truth: that covenants, being only words and breath, have no force to oblige, contain, constrain, or protect any man except what they get from the public sword — that is, from the untied hands of that man, or that assembly, who has the sovereignty, whose actions are avowed by them all and performed by the strength of them all, united in him. But when an assembly of men is made sovereign, no one imagines that any such covenant has passed at the institution. No one is so foolish as to say, for example, that the people of Rome made a covenant with the Romans to hold the sovereignty on such and such conditions — which, not performed, would have allowed the Romans lawfully to depose the Roman people. That men do not see the reasoning to be the same in a monarchy as in a popular government comes from the ambition of some, who are kinder to the government of an assembly of which they may hope to be a part than to a monarchy, which they despair of ever enjoying.
Third: No man can without injustice protest against the institution of the sovereign declared by the majority.

Because the majority by their consenting voices have declared a sovereign, he who dissented must now consent with the rest — that is, he must be content to avow whatever actions the sovereign shall do, or else justly be destroyed by the rest. For if he voluntarily entered into the congregation of those who were assembled, he sufficiently showed by that his will (and so tacitly covenanted) to stand by what the majority should ordain; and therefore if he refuses to do so, or makes any protest against any of their decrees, he acts contrary to his covenant, and so unjustly. And whether he is of the congregation or not, and whether his consent is asked or not, he must either submit to their decrees or be left in the condition of war he was in before — in which he could, without injustice, be destroyed by any man whatever.

Fourth, because by this institution every subject is the author of all the actions and judgements of the sovereign so instituted, it follows that whatever the sovereign does cannot be an injury to any of his subjects, nor ought he to be accused by any of them of injustice. For he who does anything by another's authority does no injury to the one by whose authority he acts. But by this institution of a commonwealth, every particular man is the author of all that the sovereign does; and consequently the man who complains of injury from his sovereign complains of that of which he is himself the author, and therefore ought to accuse no one but himself — nor even himself of injury, since to do injury to oneself is impossible. It is true that those who have sovereign power may commit iniquity, but not injustice, or injury, in the proper meaning of those words.

Fifth, and as a consequence of what was last said, no man who has sovereign power can justly be put to death, or otherwise in any manner punished by his subjects. For since every subject is the author of his sovereign's actions, he would be punishing another for actions committed by himself.

And because the end of this institution is the peace and defence of them all, and whoever has the right to the end has the right to the means, it belongs by right to whatever man or assembly has the sovereignty to be the judge both of the means of peace and defence, and of the hindrances and disturbances of the same — and to do whatever he shall think necessary to be done, both beforehand for preserving peace and security (by preventing discord at home and hostility from abroad) and, when peace and security are lost, for recovering them. And therefore:

Sixth, it is annexed to the sovereignty to be the judge of which opinions and doctrines are hostile to peace and which conducive to it, and consequently on what occasions, how far, and what men are to be trusted in speaking to multitudes of people, and who shall examine the doctrines of all books before they are published. For the actions of men proceed from their opinions; and in the good governing of opinions consists the good governing of men's actions, in order to their peace and concord. And though in matters of doctrine nothing ought to be regarded but the truth, this is not at odds with regulating it for the sake of peace. For doctrine contrary to peace can no more be true than peace and concord can be against the law of nature. It is true that in a commonwealth, where through the negligence or unskillfulness of governors and teachers, false doctrines have come, over time, to be generally received, the opposite truths may be generally offensive. Yet the most sudden and rough thrusting in of a new truth that can be never breaks the peace; it only sometimes wakes the war. For those men who are so loosely governed that they dare take up arms to defend or introduce an opinion are already in war; their condition is not peace but only a cessation of arms for fear of one another; and they live, as it were, perpetually on the verge of battle. It belongs therefore to the holder of sovereign power to be the judge, or to appoint all judges, of opinions and doctrines — as a thing necessary to peace, and to prevent discord and civil war.
Seventh: The right to make the rules by which each subject may know what is so much his own that no other subject may, without injustice, take it from him.

Annexed to the sovereignty is the whole power of prescribing the rules by which each man may know what goods he may enjoy, and what actions he may do, without being molested by any of his fellow subjects. And this is what men call property. For before the constitution of sovereign power (as has already been shown), all men had a right to all things; which necessarily causes war. And so this property, being necessary to peace and depending on sovereign power, is the act of that power, in the service of the public peace. These rules of property (or meum and tuum), and of good, evil, lawful, and unlawful in the actions of subjects, are the civil laws — that is, the laws of each commonwealth in particular; though the name 'civil law' is now restricted to the ancient civil laws of the city of Rome, which, being the head of a great part of the world, had laws which in our regions at that time were the civil law.

Eighth, annexed to the sovereignty is the right of judicature — that is, of hearing and deciding all controversies that may arise about law, whether civil or natural, or about fact. For without the decision of controversies, there is no protection of one subject against the injuries of another; the laws concerning meum and tuum are in vain; and each man is left, by the natural and necessary appetite for his own preservation, with the right of protecting himself by his private strength — which is the condition of war, and contrary to the end for which every commonwealth is instituted.

Ninth, annexed to the sovereignty is the right of making war and peace with other nations and commonwealths — that is, of judging when it is for the public good, and how great a force should be assembled, armed, and paid for that end, and of levying money on the subjects to cover the expenses. For the power by which the people are to be defended consists in their armies; and the strength of an army consists in the union of their strength under one command; and that command the sovereign by institution accordingly has — because command of the militia, even without any further institution, makes whoever has it sovereign. So whoever may be made general of an army, the one who has the sovereign power is always generalissimo.

Tenth, annexed to the sovereignty is the choosing of all counsellors, ministers, magistrates, and officers, in peace and in war. For since the sovereign is charged with the end — namely common peace and defence — he is understood to have the power to use such means as he shall think most fit for discharging it.
Eleventh: And of rewarding and punishing, and that (where no prior law has fixed the measure of it) at his own discretion.

To the sovereign is committed the power of rewarding with riches or honour, and of punishing with corporal or financial penalties, or with ignominy, every subject according to the law he has already made — or, where no law has been made, according as he shall judge most to conduce to encouraging men to serve the commonwealth, or to deterring them from doing it disservice.

Last, considering what values men are naturally apt to set on themselves, what respect they look for from others, and how little they value other men — from which there continually arise among them rivalry, quarrels, factions, and at last war, to the destruction of one another and the diminishing of their strength against a common enemy — it is necessary that there be laws of honour, and a public rate of worth for such men as have deserved, or are able to deserve well of the commonwealth; and that there be force in someone's hands to put those laws into execution. But it has already been shown that not only the whole militia, or armed force of the commonwealth, but also the judicature of all controversies, is annexed to the sovereignty. To the sovereign therefore it also belongs to give titles of honour, and to appoint what order of place and dignity each man shall hold, and what signs of respect men shall give to one another in public or private meetings.

These are the rights that make up the essence of sovereignty, and which are the marks by which a man may discern in which man, or assembly of men, the sovereign power is placed and resides. For these rights cannot be transferred and cannot be separated. The power to coin money; to dispose of the estate and persons of infant heirs; to have pre-emption in markets; and all other statute prerogatives may be transferred away by the sovereign, and yet the power to protect his subjects be retained. But if he transfers the militia, he retains the judicature in vain, for want of execution of the laws. Or if he grants away the power of raising money, the militia is in vain. Or if he gives away the government of doctrines, men will be frightened into rebellion by fear of spirits. And so if we consider any one of the said rights, we shall at once see that the holding of all the rest will produce no effect in preserving peace and justice — the end for which all commonwealths are instituted. This division is what is meant when it is said, 'A kingdom divided in itself cannot stand.' For unless this division comes first, division into opposing armies can never happen. If there had not first been an opinion received among most of England that these powers were divided between the king, the lords, and the House of Commons, the people would never have been divided, nor fallen into this civil war — first between those who disagreed in politics, and afterwards between the dissenters about the liberty of religion. These wars have so instructed men on this point of sovereign right that there are few now (in England) who do not see that these rights are inseparable; and this will be generally acknowledged at the next return of peace, and continue to be acknowledged until their miseries are forgotten — no longer, unless the common people are better taught than they have been until now.

And because these are essential and inseparable rights, it follows necessarily that in whatever words any of them seems to be granted away, if the sovereign power itself is not in direct terms renounced — and if the name of sovereign is no longer given by the grantees to him who grants them — the grant is void. For when he has granted all he can, if we grant the sovereignty back, all is restored, as being inseparably annexed to it.

Since this great authority is indivisible, and inseparably annexed to the sovereignty, there is little ground for the opinion of those who say of sovereign kings that, though they are singulis majores — of greater power than any one of their subjects — they are universis minores, of less power than all of them together. For if by 'all together' they do not mean the collective body taken as one person, then 'all together' and 'each one' mean the same thing, and the saying is absurd. But if by 'all together' they understand it as one person (which person the sovereign bears), then the power of 'all together' is the same as the sovereign's power; and so again the saying is absurd. They see the absurdity well enough when the sovereignty is in an assembly of the people; but in a monarch they do not see it. Yet the power of sovereignty is the same wherever it may be placed.

And as the power, so also the honour of the sovereign ought to be greater than that of any one — or all — of the subjects. For in the sovereignty is the fountain of honour. The dignities of lord, earl, duke, and prince are his creatures. As in the presence of the master, the servants are all equal, and have no honour at all, so are the subjects in the presence of the sovereign. And though they shine, some more, some less, when out of his sight, in his presence they shine no more than the stars in the presence of the sun.
Sovereign power is not as harmful as the lack of it; and the harm that comes from it, for the most part, comes from not readily submitting to a lesser harm.

But here a man may object that the condition of subjects is very miserable, since they are exposed to the lusts and other irregular passions of the man or men who have such unlimited power in their hands. And commonly those who live under a monarch think it the fault of monarchy, and those who live under a democracy or other sovereign assembly attribute every inconvenience to that form of commonwealth — whereas the power, in any of the forms, if they are sufficient to protect the subjects, is the same. They do not consider that the estate of man can never be without some inconvenience or other, and that the greatest that in any form of government can possibly happen to the people in general is scarcely felt, compared with the miseries and horrible calamities that accompany a civil war, or that dissolute condition of masterless men without subjection to laws, and without a coercive power to tie their hands from rapine and revenge. Nor do they consider that the greatest pressure of sovereign governors does not come from any delight or profit they expect from harming or weakening their subjects (in whose vigour their own strength consists), but from the subjects themselves, who, unwillingly contributing to their own defence, make it necessary for their governors to draw from them what they can in time of peace, that they may have means on any sudden emergency to resist or take advantage of their enemies. For all men are by nature equipped with notable magnifying glasses — their passions and self-love — through which every little payment appears a great grievance; but they lack those telescopes (namely moral and civil science) by which they might see at a distance the miseries that hang over them, and that cannot be avoided without such payments.

chapters.title: Chapter XIX. Of the Severall Kinds of Common-wealth by Institution, and of Succession to the Soveraigne Power
paragraphs: The difference between commonwealths consists in the difference of the sovereign, or person representing all and every one of the multitude. And since the sovereignty is either in one man, or in an assembly of more than one — and into that assembly either every man has the right to enter, or not every one but certain men set apart from the rest — it is plain that there can be only three kinds of commonwealth. For the representative must be either one man or more; and if more, then either an assembly of all, or only of a part. When the representative is one man, the commonwealth is a MONARCHY. When it is an assembly of all who choose to come together, it is a DEMOCRACY, or popular commonwealth. When it is an assembly of only a part, it is called an ARISTOCRACY. No other kind of commonwealth is possible: for either one, or more, or all must have the sovereign power (which I have shown to be indivisible) entire.

There are other names for forms of government in the histories and in books of politics — tyranny and oligarchy. But these are not names of other forms of government; they are names of the same forms, disliked. Those who are unhappy under a monarchy call it tyranny; those displeased with an aristocracy call it oligarchy; and likewise those who feel aggrieved under a democracy call it anarchy (which means absence of government) — though I think no one believes that absence of government is itself a new kind of government. By the same reasoning, men ought not to believe that the government is one kind when they like it and another when they dislike it or are oppressed by the governors.

It is plain that men who are at absolute liberty may, if they choose, give authority to one man to represent every one of them, just as they may give such authority to any assembly of men whatever; and so they may submit themselves, if they think fit, to a monarch as absolutely as to any other representative. So where a sovereign power has already been erected, no other representative of the same people can exist, except for certain particular ends, limited by the sovereign. To do otherwise would be to erect two sovereigns, and to have every man's person represented by two actors who, by opposing each other, would necessarily divide that power which (if men wish to live in peace) is indivisible, and so reduce the multitude to the condition of war — contrary to the end for which all sovereignty is instituted. And so, just as it is absurd to think that a sovereign assembly inviting the people of its dominion to send up their deputies, with power to make known their advice or wishes, should on that account hold those deputies, rather than itself, to be the absolute representative of the people, so it is absurd to think the same in a monarchy. I do not know how this so plain a truth has of late been so little observed: that in a monarchy, the man who had the sovereignty by 600 years of descent, alone called sovereign, given the title of Majesty by every one of his subjects, and unquestionably taken by them for their king, was nevertheless not considered as their representative; the name passing without contradiction to those men who, at his command, were sent up by the people to carry their petitions, and to offer him (if he permitted) their advice. This may serve as a warning to those who are the true and absolute representative of a people: to instruct men in the nature of that office, and to take care how they admit of any other general representation, on any occasion whatever, if they mean to discharge the trust committed to them.

The difference between these three kinds of commonwealth does not lie in any difference of power but in their convenience, or fitness, for producing the peace and security of the people — the end for which they were instituted. To compare monarchy with the other two, we should observe, first, that whoever bears the person of the people, or is one of the assembly that bears it, also bears his own natural person. And though in his political person he is careful to procure the common interest, he is no less — or even more — careful to procure the private good of himself, his family, his kindred, and his friends; and for the most part, if the public interest happens to clash with the private, he prefers the private. For men's passions are commonly more powerful than their reason. From this it follows that where the public and private interest are most closely united, there the public is most advanced. Now in a monarchy, the private interest is the same as the public. The riches, power, and honour of a monarch arise only from the riches, strength, and reputation of his subjects. For no king can be rich, glorious, or secure whose subjects are poor, contemptible, or too weak — through want, or through dissension — to maintain a war against their enemies. Whereas in a democracy or aristocracy, public prosperity does not contribute to the private fortune of a corrupt or ambitious man so much as does a treacherous piece of advice, a treacherous action, or a civil war.

Second, a monarch receives counsel from whomever, whenever, and wherever he pleases; and so may hear the opinions of men versed in the matter he is deliberating on, of whatever rank or quality, as long before the time of action and with as much secrecy as he wishes. But when a sovereign assembly needs counsel, none are admitted except those who have a right of admission from the start; and most of those have been versed more in the acquisition of wealth than of knowledge, and must give their advice in long speeches — which may, and commonly do, stir men to action, but do not govern them in it. For the understanding is never enlightened by the flame of the passions, but dazzled. Nor is there any place or time in which an assembly can receive counsel in secret, because of its own size.

Third, the resolutions of a monarch are subject to no inconstancy other than that of human nature. But in assemblies, besides the inconstancy of nature, there arises an inconstancy from the sheer number. The absence of a few who would have kept a resolution, once taken, firm (which may happen through complacency, negligence, or private hindrance), or the diligent appearance of a few of the opposite opinion, undoes today everything that was concluded yesterday.
Fourth, a monarch cannot disagree with himself out of envy or interest, but an assembly can — and to such a degree that it may produce a civil war.

Fifth, in monarchy there is this inconvenience: that any subject, by the power of one man, for the enriching of a favourite or flatterer, may be deprived of all he owns; which I admit is a great and unavoidable inconvenience. But the same may happen where the sovereign power is in an assembly: their power is the same; and they are as liable to evil counsel, and to being seduced by orators, as a monarch is by flatterers, and they become each other's flatterers, serving one another's covetousness and ambition in turn. And whereas the favourites of an assembly are many, and the kindred far more numerous, than those of any monarch — besides, there is no favourite of a monarch who cannot equally help his friends as harm his enemies, while orators (that is, favourites of sovereign assemblies), though they have great power to harm, have little to save. For to accuse takes less eloquence (such is man's nature) than to excuse; and condemnation more closely resembles justice than absolution does.

Sixth, it is an inconvenience in monarchy that the sovereignty may descend on an infant, or on one who cannot tell good from evil — the difficulty being that the use of his power must then be in the hand of another man, or of some assembly of men, who are to govern by his right and in his name, as guardians and protectors of his person and authority. But to say it is inconvenient to put the use of sovereign power into the hand of a man, or an assembly, is to say that all government is more inconvenient than confusion and civil war. And so all the danger that can be alleged must come from the contention of those who, for an office of such great honour and profit, may become competitors. To show that this inconvenience does not arise from the form of government we call monarchy, we should consider that the previous monarch has appointed who shall have the tutelage of his infant successor — either expressly by testament, or tacitly by not opposing the custom received in such cases. If there is then any inconvenience, it is to be attributed not to the monarchy but to the ambition and injustice of subjects; which, in every kind of government where the people are not well instructed in their duty and in the rights of sovereignty, is the same. Or else the previous monarch has made no provision at all for such tutelage; and then the law of nature has supplied this sufficient rule: that the tutelage shall be in him who by nature has the greatest interest in preserving the authority of the infant, and to whom the least benefit can come from his death or diminishment. For since every man by nature seeks his own benefit and advancement, to put an infant into the power of those who can promote themselves by his destruction or damage is not guardianship but treachery. So with sufficient provision taken against any just quarrel about the government under a child, if any contention arises that disturbs the public peace, it is not to be attributed to the form of monarchy but to the ambition of subjects and their ignorance of their duty. On the other side, there is no great commonwealth whose sovereignty is in a great assembly that is not, in matters of consultation about peace and war, and in making laws, in the same condition as if the government were in a child. For as a child lacks the judgement to dissent from counsel given him, and so is forced to take the advice of those, or of him, to whom he is committed, so an assembly lacks the liberty to dissent from the counsel of the majority, good or bad. And as a child needs a tutor or protector to preserve his person and authority, so also (in great commonwealths) the sovereign assembly, in all great dangers and troubles, has need of custodes libertatis — that is, of dictators, or protectors of their authority — which are in effect temporary monarchs, to whom for a time they may commit the entire exercise of their power; and these have, at the end of that time, been deprived of it more often than infant kings have been deprived by their protectors, regents, or other tutors.

Though the kinds of sovereignty are, as I have now shown, only three — monarchy, where one man has it; democracy, where the general assembly of subjects has it; or aristocracy, where it is in an assembly of certain persons nominated, or otherwise marked out from the rest — yet anyone who considers the particular commonwealths that have existed, and that exist, in the world may not easily reduce them to three, and may be inclined to think there are other forms, arising from these mixed together. For example: elective kingdoms, where kings have the sovereign power put into their hands for a time; or kingdoms in which the king has a limited power. Such governments are nevertheless called monarchies by most writers. Likewise, if a popular or aristocratic commonwealth subdues an enemy's country and governs it by a president, procurator, or other magistrate, this may at first sight seem to be a democratic or aristocratic government. But it is not. For elective kings are not sovereigns but ministers of the sovereign; nor are limited kings sovereigns, but ministers of those who hold the sovereign power; nor are provinces subject to a democracy or aristocracy of another commonwealth governed democratically or aristocratically, but monarchically.

And first, concerning an elective king whose power is limited to his life, as it is in many parts of Christendom today, or to a certain number of years or months, as the Dictator's power was at Rome: if he has the right to appoint his successor, he is no longer elective but hereditary. But if he has no power to elect his successor, then there must be some other man, or known assembly, that may after his death elect a new one — or else the commonwealth dies and dissolves with him, and returns to the condition of war. If it is known who have the power to give the sovereignty after his death, it is known also that the sovereignty was in them before; for no one has the right to give what he has no right to possess and to keep to himself, if he thinks fit. But if there is no one who can give the sovereignty after the death of the first elected, then he himself has the power — indeed he is obliged by the law of nature — to provide, by appointing his successor, against the people who trusted him with the government slipping back into the miserable condition of civil war. And consequently he was, when elected, an absolute sovereign.

Second: a king whose power is limited is not superior to him, or to them, who have the power to limit it; and one who is not superior is not supreme — that is, not sovereign. The sovereignty therefore was always in that assembly which had the right to limit him; and so the government was not monarchy but either democracy or aristocracy. So it was in ancient Sparta, where the kings had the privilege of leading their armies but the sovereignty was in the Ephors.

Third, whereas in former times the Roman people governed (for example) the land of Judea by a president, Judea was not therefore a democracy, because the Jews were not governed by any assembly which any of them had the right to enter; nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by any assembly which any man could enter by their election. They were governed by one person, who though to the people of Rome was an assembly of the people, or democracy, was as far as the people of Judea were concerned — who had no right at all to participate in the government — a monarch. For though where the people are governed by an assembly chosen by themselves out of their own number, the government is called democracy or aristocracy, when they are governed by an assembly not of their own choosing, it is a monarchy: not of one man over another man, but of one people over another people.

In every one of these forms of government, the matter being mortal — so that not only monarchs but whole assemblies die — it is necessary for preserving the peace among men that, just as order was taken for an artificial man, so also order should be taken for an artificial eternity of life. Without that, men who are governed by an assembly would return into the condition of war in every age, and those who are governed by one man as soon as their governor dies. This artificial eternity is what men call the right of succession.

No form of government is perfect where the disposing of the succession is not in the present sovereign. For if it is in any other particular man, or in any private assembly, it is in a person who is a subject, and may be assumed by the sovereign at his pleasure — and so the right is in himself. And if it is in no particular man, but left to a new choice, then the commonwealth is dissolved, and the right is in whoever can seize it; contrary to the intention of those who instituted the commonwealth for their perpetual, not temporary, security.
In a democracy, the whole assembly cannot fail unless the multitude that is to be governed fails. And so questions of the right of succession have no place at all in that form of government.

In an aristocracy, when any member of the assembly dies, the election of another to fill his place belongs to the assembly, as the sovereign — to whom belongs the choosing of all counsellors and officers. For what the representative does as actor, every one of the subjects does as author. And though the sovereign assembly may give power to others to elect new men to fill its ranks, the election is still made by its authority; and by the same authority it may, when the public requires, be recalled.

The present monarch has the right to dispose of the succession. The greatest difficulty about the right of succession is in monarchy; and the difficulty arises from this: that at first sight it is not clear who is to appoint the successor, nor often who it is whom he has appointed. For in both these matters a more exact reasoning is needed than every man is used to. As for the question of who shall appoint the successor of a monarch holding sovereign authority (that is — for elective kings and princes do not hold the sovereign power as property but only in use), we must consider that either the man in possession has the right to dispose of the succession, or that right is once again in the dissolved multitude. For the death of him who holds the sovereign power as his property leaves the multitude without any sovereign at all — that is, without any representative in whom they may be united and capable of doing any single action. They are therefore incapable of electing a new monarch; every man having equal right to submit himself to whoever he thinks best able to protect him, or if he can, to protect himself by his own sword. Which is a return to confusion and to the condition of a war of every man against every man, contrary to the end for which monarchy had its first institution. So it is plain that by the institution of monarchy, the disposing of the successor is always left to the judgement and will of the present possessor.

And as for the question (which may sometimes arise) of who it is that the monarch in possession has designated for the succession and inheritance of his power, this is settled by his express words and testament, or by other tacit signs that are sufficient.

By express words, or by testament, when he declares it in his lifetime, viva voce or in writing — as the first emperors of Rome declared who should be their heirs. For the word 'heir' does not in itself imply the children, or nearest kindred, of a man; it means whoever a man shall in any way declare he wishes to succeed him in his estate. If therefore a monarch expressly declares, by word or in writing, that such a man shall be his heir, then that man is immediately on the death of his predecessor invested in the right of being monarch.

But where testament and express words are wanting, other natural signs of his will are to be followed; one of which is custom. So where the custom is that the next of kin succeeds absolutely, there also the next of kin has the right to the succession; because if the will of the man who was in possession had been otherwise, he could easily have declared the same in his lifetime. And likewise where the custom is that the next of the male kindred succeeds, there too the right of succession is in the next male kinsman, for the same reason. And so it is also if the custom were to advance the female. For whatever custom a man may by a word override, and does not, is a natural sign that he would have the custom stand.

But where neither custom nor testament has gone before, it is to be understood, first, that a monarch's will is that the government remain monarchical, because he has approved that form of government in himself. Second, that a child of his own, male or female, is to be preferred to any other; because men are presumed to be more inclined by nature to advance their own children than the children of other men — and, of their own, rather a male than a female, because men are naturally fitter than women for actions of labour and danger. Third, where his own issue fails, a brother is preferred over a stranger, and the closer in blood over the more remote; because it is always presumed that the nearer of kin is the nearer in affection. And it is evident that a man always receives, by reflection, the most honour from the greatness of his closest kin.

But if it is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by words of contract or by testament, men may perhaps object a great inconvenience: that he may sell, or give, his right of governing to a stranger; which, because strangers (that is, men not used to living under the same government, not speaking the same language) commonly undervalue one another, may turn to the oppression of his subjects. This is indeed a great inconvenience; but it does not necessarily follow from subjection to a stranger's government, but from the unskillfulness of the governors, ignorant of the true rules of politics. And so the Romans, when they had subdued many nations, in order to make their government digestible, used to remove that grievance as far as they thought necessary by giving, sometimes to whole nations, and sometimes to the principal men of every nation they conquered, not only the privileges but also the name of Romans, and by taking many of them into the Senate and into offices of charge, even in the city of Rome itself. This was what our most wise king, King James, aimed at in seeking the union of his two realms of England and Scotland. If he could have achieved it, in all likelihood it would have prevented the civil wars that make both those kingdoms now miserable. So it is no injury to the people for a monarch to dispose of the succession by will, though by the fault of many princes it has sometimes proved inconvenient. As another argument for its lawfulness: whatever inconvenience may come from giving a kingdom to a stranger may also come from marrying so with strangers that the right of succession may descend to them — yet this is by everyone accounted lawful.

chapters.title: Chapter XX. Of Dominion Paternall and Despoticall
paragraphs: A commonwealth by acquisition is one in which the sovereign power is acquired by force. It is acquired by force when men, either singly or many together by plurality of votes, for fear of death or bondage, authorise all the actions of the man, or assembly, who holds their lives and liberty in his power.

This kind of dominion, or sovereignty, differs from sovereignty by institution only in this: that men who choose their sovereign do it from fear of one another, and not from fear of him whom they institute; whereas in this case they subject themselves to the man they are afraid of. In both cases they act from fear — which should be noted by those who hold that all such covenants as proceed from fear of death or violence are void. If that were so, no man in any kind of commonwealth could be obliged to obedience. It is true that in a commonwealth once instituted or acquired, promises proceeding from fear of death or violence are no covenants, and do not oblige, when the thing promised is contrary to the laws. But the reason is not that the promise was made under fear; it is that the person promising had no right in the thing promised. Also, when a man may lawfully perform a promise and does not, what releases him is not the invalidity of the covenant, but the sentence of the sovereign. Otherwise, whenever a man lawfully promised, he would unlawfully break — but when the sovereign, who is the actor, acquits him, then he is acquitted by the one who extorted the promise, as by the author of such release.

But the rights and consequences of sovereignty are the same in both. The sovereign's power cannot, without his consent, be transferred to another; he cannot forfeit it; he cannot be accused by any of his subjects of injury; he cannot be punished by them; he is the judge of what is necessary for peace, and judge of doctrines; he is sole legislator, and supreme judge of controversies, and of the times and occasions of war and peace. To him belongs the choice of magistrates, counsellors, commanders, and all other officers and ministers, and the determination of rewards and punishments, of honour and order. The reasons for all this are the same as those given in the previous chapter for the same rights and consequences of sovereignty by institution.

Dominion is acquired in two ways: by generation, and by conquest. The right of dominion by generation is the right a parent has over his children, and is called PATERNAL. And it is not derived from generation in such a way that the parent has dominion over his child merely because he begot him; it comes from the child's consent, either expressed or declared by other sufficient signs. As to generation, God has ordained for man a helper, and there are always two who are equally parents. Dominion over the child therefore should belong equally to both, and the child be equally subject to both — which is impossible, for no man can obey two masters. And whereas some have attributed the dominion to the man only, as being of the more excellent sex, they miscalculate. There is not always such a difference of strength or prudence between man and woman that the right can be settled without war. In commonwealths this controversy is decided by the civil law, and for the most part (though not always) the sentence is in favour of the father, because for the most part commonwealths have been founded by the fathers, not by the mothers, of families. But the question now lies in the state of mere nature, where there are supposed no laws of matrimony, no laws for the education of children — only the law of nature, and the natural inclination of the sexes to each other and to their children. In this condition of mere nature, either the parents between themselves dispose of the dominion over the child by contract, or they do not. If they do, the right passes according to the contract. We find in history that the Amazons contracted with the men of the neighbouring countries, to whom they resorted for offspring, that the male issue should be sent back to the fathers but the female should remain with them; so the dominion of the females was in the mother.

If there is no contract, the dominion is in the mother. For in the condition of mere nature, where there are no matrimonial laws, it cannot be known who the father is unless the mother declares it; and so the right of dominion over the child depends on her will, and is consequently hers. Further: the infant is first in the mother's power — she may nourish it or expose it. If she nourishes it, it owes its life to her, and is therefore obliged to obey her rather than any other; and so dominion over it is hers. But if she exposes it and another finds and nourishes it, the dominion is in the one who nourishes it. The child should obey the one who preserves it, because the preservation of life being the end for which one man becomes subject to another, every man is presumed to promise obedience to the one in whose power it lies to save or destroy him.

If the mother is the father's subject, the child is in the father's power; and if the father is the mother's subject (as when a sovereign queen marries one of her subjects), the child is subject to the mother, because the father too is her subject.

If a man and a woman, monarchs of two distinct kingdoms, have a child, and contract concerning who shall have the dominion over him, the right of dominion passes by the contract. If they make no contract, the dominion follows the dominion of the place of his residence: for the sovereign of each country has dominion over all who reside in it.

He who has dominion over the child has dominion also over the children's children. For he who has dominion over the person of a man has dominion over all that is his — without which, dominion would be only a title, without effect.
The right of succession to paternal dominion runs the same way as the right of succession to monarchy, of which I have already said enough in the previous chapter.

Dominion acquired by conquest, or by victory in war, is what some writers call DESPOTICAL, from despotes, which means a lord or master; it is the dominion of master over servant. This dominion is acquired by the victor when the vanquished, to avoid the present stroke of death, covenants either in express words or by other sufficient signs of the will that, so long as his life and the liberty of his body are allowed him, the victor shall have the use of them at his pleasure. And after such a covenant is made, the vanquished is a SERVANT — and not before. For by the word 'servant' (whether derived from servire, to serve, or from servare, to save — which I leave to grammarians to dispute) is not meant a captive kept in prison or in bonds until the master who took him, or who bought him from one who did, shall decide what to do with him. Such men, commonly called slaves, are under no obligation at all, and may justly break their bonds or the prison, and kill or carry away captive their master. 'Servant' here means rather one who, being taken, has been allowed bodily liberty, and on his promise neither to run away nor to do violence to his master, is trusted by him.

It is not therefore the victory that gives the right of dominion over the vanquished, but the vanquished man's own covenant. Nor is he obliged because he is conquered — that is, beaten and taken, or put to flight — but because he comes in and submits to the victor. Nor is the victor obliged, by an enemy's surrendering (without any promise of life), to spare him for that surrender to discretion: it obliges the victor no longer than as, in his own discretion, he shall think fit.

What men do when they ask (as it is now called) for quarter — what the Greeks called zogria, taking alive — is to evade the immediate fury of the victor by submission, and to compound for their life with ransom or service. And so the man who has quarter has not had his life given but deferred until further consideration. It is not a surrender on condition of life, but a surrender to discretion. His life is only then secure, and his service only then due, when the victor has trusted him with bodily liberty. For slaves who work in prisons or in fetters do not do so out of duty, but to avoid the cruelty of their taskmasters.

The master of the servant is also master of all the servant has, and may exact the use of it — that is, of his goods, his labour, his servants, and his children — as often as he thinks fit. For the servant holds his life from his master by the covenant of obedience: that is, by owning and authorising whatever the master shall do. And if the master, when the servant refuses, kills him, or casts him into bonds, or otherwise punishes him for his disobedience, the servant is himself the author of it, and cannot accuse him of injury.

In short, the rights and consequences of both paternal and despotical dominion are exactly the same as those of a sovereign by institution, and for the same reasons, which are set down in the previous chapter. So for a man who is monarch of several nations — having in one the sovereignty by institution of the people assembled, and in another by conquest, that is by the submission of each individual to avoid death or bondage — to demand more from the one nation than from the other on grounds of conquest, as being a conquered nation, is an act of ignorance of the rights of sovereignty. For the sovereign is absolute over both alike, or else there is no sovereignty at all; and so every man may lawfully protect himself, if he can, with his own sword — which is the condition of war.

By this it appears that a great family, if it is not part of some commonwealth, is in itself, as to the rights of sovereignty, a little monarchy — whether that family consists of a man and his children, of a man and his servants, or of a man with his children and servants together; in which the father, or master, is the sovereign. Yet a family is not properly a commonwealth, unless it is of such power, by its own numbers or by other opportunities, that it cannot be subdued without the hazard of war. For where a body of men is plainly too weak to defend themselves united, every one may use his own reason in time of danger to save his own life, either by flight or by submission to the enemy, as he shall think best — just as a very small company of soldiers surprised by an army may throw down their arms and ask for quarter, or run away, rather than be put to the sword. And so much shall suffice for what I find by speculation and deduction concerning sovereign rights, drawn from the nature, needs, and designs of men in erecting commonwealths and putting themselves under monarchs or assemblies entrusted with power enough for their protection.

Let us now consider what Scripture teaches on the same point. To Moses, the children of Israel say: 'Speak thou to us, and we will hear thee; but let not God speak to us, lest we die' (Exodus 20:19). This is absolute obedience to Moses. Concerning the right of kings, God himself, by the mouth of Samuel, says (1 Samuel 8:11–12 etc.): 'This shall be the right of the king you will have to reign over you. He shall take your sons, and set them to drive his chariots, and to be his horsemen, and to run before his chariots; and gather in his harvest; and to make his engines of war, and instruments of his chariots; and shall take your daughters to make perfumes, to be his cooks and bakers. He shall take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive yards, and give them to his servants. He shall take the tithe of your corn and wine, and give it to the men of his chamber, and to his other servants. He shall take your manservants, and your maidservants, and the choice of your youth, and employ them in his business. He shall take the tithe of your flocks; and you shall be his servants.' This is absolute power, summed up in the last words: 'you shall be his servants.' Again, when the people heard what power their king was to have, they still consented, saying (verse 19 etc.): 'We will be as all other nations, and our king shall judge our causes, and go before us, to conduct our wars.' Here is confirmed the right that sovereigns have, both to the militia and to all judicature — which contains as absolute a power as one man can possibly transfer to another. Again, King Solomon's prayer to God was this (1 Kings 3:9): 'Give to thy servant understanding, to judge thy people, and to discern between good and evil.' It belongs therefore to the sovereign to be judge, and to prescribe the rules of discerning good and evil; and these rules are laws; and so in him is the legislative power. Saul sought David's life; yet when it was in David's power to slay Saul, and his servants would have done it, David forbade them, saying (1 Samuel 24:9): 'God forbid I should do such an act against my lord, the anointed of God.' For the obedience of servants, St Paul says (Colossians 3:22): 'Servants, obey your masters in all things,' and (verse 20): 'Children, obey your parents in all things.' That is plain obedience in those who are subject to paternal or despotical dominion. Again (Matthew 23:2–3): 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' chair, and therefore all that they shall bid you observe, that observe and do.' There again is plain obedience. And St Paul (Titus 3:1): 'Warn them that they subject themselves to princes, and to those that are in authority, and obey them.' This obedience is also plain. Lastly, our Saviour himself acknowledges that men ought to pay such taxes as kings impose, when he says, 'Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's' — and paid such taxes himself. And that the king's word is enough to take anything from any subject when there is need, and that the king is judge of that need: for he himself, as king of the Jews, ordered his disciples to take the ass and the ass's colt to carry him into Jerusalem, saying (Matthew 21:2–3): 'Go into the village over against you, and you shall find an ass tied, and her colt with her; loose them, and bring them to me. And if any man asks you what you mean by it, say, The Lord has need of them; and they will let them go.' They are not to ask whether his necessity is a sufficient title, nor whether he is the judge of that necessity, but to acquiesce in the will of the Lord.

To these passages may also be added the one in Genesis (3:5): 'You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil'; and verse 11: 'Who told thee that thou wast naked? hast thou eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee thou shouldest not eat?' The faculty of judging good and evil, being forbidden under the name of the fruit of the tree of knowledge as a test of Adam's obedience, was the very thing the devil, to inflame the ambition of the woman (to whom that fruit already seemed beautiful), promised they would obtain by tasting it: that they should be as gods, knowing good and evil. Having both eaten, they did indeed take upon themselves God's office, which is the judicature of good and evil; but they acquired no new ability to distinguish rightly between them. And as for the saying that, having eaten, they saw they were naked, no one has interpreted that passage as if they had previously been blind and unable to see their own skins. The meaning is plain: it was then that they first judged their nakedness (in which it was God's will to create them) to be unseemly; and by being ashamed, they tacitly censured God himself. And thereupon God says, 'Hast thou eaten? etc.' — as if to say, 'Do you, who owe me obedience, take it upon yourself to judge of my commandments?' By which it is clearly, though allegorically, signified that the commands of those who have the right to command are not to be censured, or disputed, by their subjects.

So it plainly appears, to my understanding, both from reason and from Scripture, that the sovereign power — whether placed in one man, as in monarchy, or in one assembly of men, as in popular and aristocratic commonwealths — is as great as men can possibly imagine making it. And though men may fancy many evil consequences from so unlimited a power, the consequences of the lack of it — which is perpetual war of every man against his neighbour — are much worse. The condition of man in this life shall never be without inconveniences; but no great inconvenience happens in any commonwealth that does not proceed from the subjects' disobedience and breach of those covenants from which the commonwealth had its being. And whoever, thinking sovereign power too great, will seek to make it less, must subject himself to the power that can limit it — that is, to a greater.

The greatest objection is from practice, when men ask where, and when, such power has been acknowledged by subjects. But one may ask them in turn: when, or where, has there been a kingdom long free from sedition and civil war? In those nations whose commonwealths have been long-lived and have been destroyed only by foreign war, the subjects never disputed the sovereign power. In any case, an argument from the practice of men who have not sifted the matter to the bottom, and who have not by exact reasoning weighed the causes and nature of commonwealths, and who suffer daily the miseries that come from ignorance of these things, is invalid. For though in every part of the world men should lay the foundations of their houses on the sand, it could not be inferred from that that this is how it should be done. The skill of building and maintaining commonwealths consists in certain rules, as does arithmetic and geometry; not (as a game of tennis does) on practice alone. These rules neither poor men have had the leisure, nor men who have had the leisure have hitherto had the curiosity, or the method, to find out.

chapters.title: Chapter XXI. Of the Liberty of Subjects
paragraphs: Liberty, or FREEDOM, properly signifies the absence of opposition — by which I mean external impediments to motion — and may be applied no less to irrational and inanimate things than to rational ones. For whatever is so tied, or hemmed in, that it cannot move except within a certain space, that space being determined by the opposition of some external body, we say it has no liberty to go further. So of all living creatures, while they are imprisoned or restrained with walls or chains; and of water, while it is held in by banks or vessels which otherwise would spread it into a larger space, we say they are not at liberty to move in the way they would without those external obstacles. But when the impediment to motion is in the constitution of the thing itself, we do not say it lacks liberty, but the power to move — as when a stone lies still, or a man is bound to his bed by sickness.

And according to this proper and generally received meaning of the word, a FREE-MAN is 'he who, in the things he is able by his strength and wit to do, is not hindered from doing what he has a will to do.' But when the words 'free' and 'liberty' are applied to anything but bodies, they are misused; for what is not subject to motion is not subject to impediment. So when it is said (for example) 'the way is free,' no liberty of the way is meant, but of those who walk in it without being stopped. When we say a gift is free, no liberty of the gift is meant but of the giver, who was not bound by any law or covenant to give it. So when we speak freely, it is not the liberty of voice or pronunciation, but of the man, whom no law has obliged to speak otherwise than he did. Finally, from the phrase 'free will' no liberty can be inferred to the will, desire, or inclination, but only to the man — which consists in this, that he finds no obstacle in doing what he has the will, the desire, or the inclination to do.

Fear and liberty are consistent. When a man throws his goods into the sea for fear that the ship may sink, he nevertheless does it very willingly, and may refuse to do it if he wishes; it is therefore the action of someone who was free. Likewise, a man sometimes pays his debt only for fear of imprisonment — and since no one was hindering him from keeping it back, it was the action of a man at liberty. In general, all actions which men do in commonwealths for fear of the law are actions the doers had the liberty to omit.

Liberty and necessity are consistent. As in water, which has not only the liberty but also the necessity of running down the channel, so also in the actions men voluntarily do: those actions, because they proceed from their will, proceed from liberty; and yet, because every act of a man's will, and every desire and inclination, proceeds from some cause — and those causes, in a continual chain (whose first link is in the hand of God, the first of all causes), proceed from necessity. So to one who could see the connection of those causes, the necessity of all men's voluntary actions would appear plain. And so God, who sees and disposes all things, sees also that man's liberty in doing what he wills is accompanied by the necessity of doing what God wills, and no more and no less. For though men may do many things which God does not command, and of which he is not therefore the author, they can have no passion or appetite for anything of which God's will is not the cause. And if his will did not secure the necessity of man's will, and consequently of everything that depends on man's will, the liberty of men would be a contradiction and an impediment to the omnipotence and the liberty of God. And so much (as far as the matter at hand) for that natural liberty, which alone is properly called liberty.

But as men, in order to attain peace and so to preserve themselves, have made an artificial man (which we call a commonwealth), so they have also made artificial chains, called civil laws, which they themselves, by mutual covenants, have fastened at one end to the lips of that man, or assembly, to whom they have given the sovereign power, and at the other end to their own ears. These bonds, weak in themselves, may nevertheless be made to hold by the danger, even where not by the difficulty, of breaking them.

It is only in relation to these bonds that I am now to speak of the liberty of subjects. Since there is no commonwealth in the world that can regulate every action and every word of men (that being impossible), it follows necessarily that in all kinds of action which the laws have passed over, men have the liberty of doing what their own reason shall suggest as most profitable to themselves. For if we take liberty in its proper sense — bodily liberty, that is, freedom from chains and prison — it would be very absurd for men to clamour, as they do, for a liberty they so plainly already enjoy. Again, if we take liberty as exemption from the laws, it is no less absurd for men to demand, as they do, a liberty by which all other men might be masters of their lives. And yet, absurd as it is, this is what they demand — not knowing that the laws have no power to protect them without a sword in the hands of a man, or men, to cause those laws to be executed. The liberty of a subject lies therefore only in those things which, in regulating their actions, the sovereign has passed over — such as the liberty to buy and sell, and otherwise to contract with one another, to choose their own dwelling, their own diet, their own trade of life, and to bring up their children as they themselves think fit, and the like.

Nevertheless, we are not to understand that by such liberty the sovereign power of life and death is either abolished or limited.
