For there was never any but the high priest only who was to inform the people of God's will; nor was any convocation of priests ever allowed to enter into the Sanctum Sanctorum.

Again, the title of a 'holy nation' confirms the same. For 'holy' signifies that which is God's by special, not by general, right. All the earth (as is said in the text) is God's; but all the earth is not called holy — only that which is set apart for his special service, as the nation of the Jews was. It is therefore plain enough by this one passage that by the kingdom of God is properly meant a commonwealth, instituted (by the consent of those who were to be subject to it) for their civil government, and for the regulating of their behaviour not only toward God their king, but also toward one another in point of justice, and toward other nations both in peace and in war; which was properly a kingdom, in which God was king and the high priest was to be (after the death of Moses) his sole viceroy, or lieutenant.

But there are many other places that clearly prove the same. First (1 Sam. 8:7), when the elders of Israel (grieved by the corruption of the sons of Samuel) demanded a king, Samuel was displeased with this, and prayed to the Lord; and the Lord, answering, said to him: 'Listen to the voice of the people, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.' From which it is evident that God himself was then their king; and that Samuel did not command the people, but only delivered to them what God from time to time appointed him.

Again, (1 Sam. 12:12), where Samuel says to the people: 'When you saw that Nahash, king of the children of Ammon, came against you, you said to me, Nay, but a king shall reign over us — when the Lord your God was your king.' It is plain that God was their king, and governed the civil state of their commonwealth.

And after the Israelites had rejected God, the prophets foretold his restoration. As in Isaiah 24:23: 'Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem' — where he speaks expressly of his reign in Zion and Jerusalem; that is, on earth. And (Micah 4:7), 'And the Lord shall reign over them in Mount Zion'; this Mount Zion is in Jerusalem, on the earth. And (Ezek. 20:33), 'As I live, says the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, I will rule over you'; and (verse 37) 'I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant' — that is, 'I will reign over you, and make you stand to that covenant which you made with me by Moses, and broke in your rebellion against me in the days of Samuel, and in your election of another king.'

And in the New Testament, the angel Gabriel says of our Saviour (Luke 1:32–33): 'He shall be great, and be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord shall give him the throne of his father David; and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.' This is also a kingdom on earth; for the claim of which, as an enemy to Caesar, he was put to death. The title of his cross was 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews'; he was crowned in scorn with a crown of thorns; and for the proclaiming of him it is said of the disciples (Acts 17:7) that 'they did all of them contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying there was another king, one Jesus.' The kingdom therefore of God is a real, not a metaphorical, kingdom — and so taken not only in the Old Testament but in the New. When we say, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory,' it is to be understood of God's kingdom by force of our covenant, not by the right of God's power; for such a kingdom God always has. So it would be superfluous to say in our prayer, 'Your kingdom come,' unless it is meant of the restoration of that kingdom of God by Christ which by the revolt of the Israelites had been interrupted at the election of Saul. Nor would it have been proper to say 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand,' or to pray 'Your kingdom come,' if it had still continued.

There are so many other places that confirm this interpretation that it would be a wonder no greater notice is taken of it — except that it gives too much light to Christian kings to see their right of ecclesiastical government. This is what those have observed who, in place of 'sacerdotal kingdom,' translate 'a kingdom of priests'; for they may as well translate 'royal priesthood' (as it is in St Peter) into 'a priesthood of kings.' And whereas, for 'peculiar people,' they put 'precious jewel,' or 'treasure,' a man might as well call the special regiment, or company, of a general the general's 'precious jewel,' or his 'treasure.'

In short, the kingdom of God is a civil kingdom; which consisted first in the obligation of the people of Israel to those laws which Moses should bring to them from Mount Sinai, and which afterwards the high priest of the time being should deliver to them from before the cherubim in the Sanctum Sanctorum; and which kingdom, having been cast off at the election of Saul, the prophets foretold should be restored by Christ. And the restoration of it we daily pray for, when we say in the Lord's Prayer, 'Your kingdom come'; and the right of it we acknowledge, when we add, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, amen'; and the proclaiming of it was the preaching of the apostles. To which men are prepared by the teachers of the gospel; to embrace which gospel (that is, to promise obedience to God's government) is to be in the kingdom of grace, because God has gratis given to such the power to be the subjects (that is, children) of God hereafter, when Christ shall come in majesty to judge the world, and actually to govern his own people — which is called the kingdom of glory. If the kingdom of God (also called the kingdom of heaven, from the gloriousness and admirable height of that throne) were not a kingdom which God, by his lieutenant or vicars, who deliver his commandments to the people, did exercise on earth, there would not have been so much contention and war about who it is by whom God speaks to us; nor would many priests have troubled themselves with spiritual jurisdiction, nor any king have denied it to them.

Out of this literal interpretation of the kingdom of God arises also the true interpretation of the word HOLY. For it is a word which in God's kingdom answers to that which men in their kingdoms use to call 'public,' or 'the king's.'

The king of any country is the public person, or representative, of all his own subjects. And God, the king of Israel, was the Holy One of Israel. The nation which is subject to one earthly sovereign is the nation of that sovereign — that is, of the public person. So the Jews, who were God's nation, were called (Exod. 19:6) 'a holy nation.' For by 'holy' is always understood either God himself, or what is God's in property; as by 'public' is always meant either the person of the commonwealth itself, or something that is so the commonwealth's that no private person can claim any property in it.

Therefore the Sabbath (God's day) is a holy day; the temple (God's house) a holy house; sacrifices, tithes, and offerings (God's tribute) holy duties; priests, prophets, and anointed kings under Christ (God's ministers) holy men; the celestial ministering spirits (God's messengers) holy angels; and the like. Wherever the word 'holy' is taken properly, there is always signified something of property, gotten by consent. In saying 'Hallowed be your name,' we do but pray to God for grace to keep the first commandment, of 'having no other gods but Him.' Mankind is God's nation in general, but the Jews only were a holy nation. Why? Because they became his property by covenant.

And the word 'profane' is usually taken in Scripture for the same as 'common'; and consequently their contraries, 'holy' and 'proper,' in the kingdom of God must be the same also. But figuratively, those men too are called holy who led such godly lives that it was as though they had forsaken all worldly designs, and wholly devoted, and given, themselves to God. In the proper sense, what is made holy by God's appropriating or separating it to his own use is said to be sanctified by God — as the seventh day in the fourth commandment; and as the elect in the New Testament were said to be sanctified when they were endowed with the spirit of godliness. And what is made holy by the dedication of men, and given to God so as to be used only in his public service, is also called SACRED, and said to be consecrated — as temples and other houses of public prayer, and their utensils, priests, and ministers, victims, offerings, and the external matter of the sacraments.

Of holiness there are degrees. For of those things set apart for the service of God, some may be set apart again, for a nearer and more especial service. The whole nation of the Israelites were a people holy to God; yet the tribe of Levi was, among the Israelites, a holy tribe; and among the Levites, the priests were yet more holy; and among the priests, the high priest was the most holy. So the land of Judea was the Holy Land; but the holy city in which God was to be worshipped was more holy; and again, the temple more holy than the city; and the Sanctum Sanctorum more holy than the rest of the temple.

A SACRAMENT is a setting apart of some visible thing from common use, and a consecration of it to God's service, for a sign — either of our admission into the kingdom of God, to be of the number of his peculiar people, or as a commemoration of the same. In the Old Testament, the sign of admission was circumcision; in the New Testament, baptism. The commemoration of it in the Old Testament was the eating (at a certain time, which was annual) of the paschal lamb, by which they were reminded of the night in which they were delivered out of their bondage in Egypt; and in the New Testament, the celebrating of the Lord's Supper, by which we are reminded of our deliverance from the bondage of sin, by our blessed Saviour's death on the cross. The sacraments of admission are to be used only once, because only one admission is needed; but because we have need of being often reminded of our deliverance, and of our allegiance, the sacraments of commemoration need to be repeated. These are the principal sacraments — as it were, the solemn oaths we make of our allegiance. There are also other consecrations that may be called sacraments, as the word implies only consecration to God's service; but as it implies an oath, or promise, of allegiance to God, there were no others in the Old Testament except circumcision and the Passover, nor are there any others in the New Testament except baptism and the Lord's Supper.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVI. Of the Word of God, and of Prophets
paragraphs: When there is mention of the word of God, or of man, it does not signify a part of speech such as grammarians call a noun or a verb, or any simple sound without a context of other words to make it meaningful, but a perfect speech or discourse by which the speaker affirms, denies, commands, promises, threatens, wishes, or asks. In this sense it is not vocabulum that means a word, but sermo (in Greek logos) — some speech, discourse, or saying.

Again, when we say 'the word of God,' or 'of man,' it may sometimes be understood of the speaker (as the words that God has spoken, or that a man has spoken). In that sense, when we say 'the Gospel of St Matthew,' we understand St Matthew to be the writer of it. And sometimes it is understood of the subject: in this sense, when we read in the Bible 'The words of the days of the kings of Israel, or of Judah,' it is meant that the acts done in those days were the subject of those 'words.' And in the Greek, which (in Scripture) retains many Hebraisms, by 'the word of God' is often meant not what is spoken by God, but what is spoken concerning God, and his government — that is, the doctrine of religion. So much so that to say logos theou and theologia is all one — which is the doctrine we usually call divinity, as is plain from the following passages. Acts 13:46: 'Then Paul and Barnabas grew bold, and said: It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you; but seeing you put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.' What is here called the word of God was the doctrine of the Christian religion, as is evident from what goes before. And in Acts 5:20, where it is said to the apostles by an angel, 'Go, stand and speak in the temple, all the words of this life' — by 'the words of this life' is meant the doctrine of the gospel, as is evident from what they did in the temple, and is expressed in the last verse of the same chapter: 'Daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Christ Jesus.' From this it is plain that Jesus Christ was the subject of this 'word of life,' or (which is all one) the subject of the 'words of this life eternal' that our Saviour offered them. So (Acts 15:7) the word of God is called the word of the gospel, because it contains the doctrine of the kingdom of Christ; and the same word (Rom. 10:8–9) is called the word of faith — that is, as is there explained, the doctrine of Christ come, and raised from the dead. Also (Matt. 13:19): 'When any one hears the word of the kingdom,' that is, the doctrine of the kingdom taught by Christ. Again, the same word is said (Acts 12:24) to 'grow and to be multiplied'; which to understand of the evangelical doctrine is easy, but of the voice or speech of God, hard and strange. In the same sense the 'doctrine of devils' signifies not the words of any devil, but the doctrine of heathen men concerning daemons, and those phantasms which they worshipped as gods (1 Tim. 4:1).

Considering these two meanings of the WORD OF GOD as it is taken in Scripture, it is plain in this latter sense (where it is taken for the doctrine of the Christian religion) that the whole Scripture is the word of God; but in the former sense not so. For example, though the words 'I am the Lord your God, etc.' to the end of the Ten Commandments were spoken by God to Moses, the preface 'God spoke these words and said' is to be understood as the words of the one who wrote the holy history. The word of God, as it is taken for what he has spoken, is understood sometimes properly, sometimes metaphorically. Properly, as the words he has spoken to his prophets; metaphorically, for his wisdom, power, and eternal decree in making the world — in which sense, those Fiats, 'Let there be light,' 'Let there be a firmament,' 'Let us make man,' and so on (Genesis 1), are the word of God. And in the same sense it is said (John 1:3) that 'all things were made by it, and without it was nothing made that was made'; and (Heb. 1:3) 'He upholds all things by the word of his power' — that is, by the power of his word, that is, by his power; and (Heb. 11:3) 'The worlds were framed by the word of God'; and many other passages to the same sense. So also among the Latins, the name 'fate,' which means properly the word spoken, is taken in the same sense.

Second, for the effect of his word — that is, for the thing itself which by his word is affirmed, commanded, threatened, or promised. As in Psalm 105:19, where Joseph is said to have been kept in prison 'till his word was come' — that is, till what he had (Gen. 40:13) foretold to Pharaoh's butler, concerning his being restored to his office, had come to pass. There, 'his word was come' means the thing itself had come to pass. So also (1 Kings 18:36) Elijah says to God, 'I have done all these your words,' instead of 'I have done all these things at your word,' or commandment. And (Jer. 17:15), 'Where is the word of the Lord?' is put for 'Where is the evil he threatened?' And (Ezek. 12:28), 'There shall none of my words be prolonged any more' — by 'words' are meant the things God promised to his people. And in the New Testament (Matt. 24:35), 'Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away' — that is, there is nothing I have promised or foretold that shall not come to pass. And in this sense it is that St John the Evangelist — and, I think, St John alone — calls our Saviour himself, in the flesh, 'the Word of God,' as in John 1:14: 'The Word was made flesh.' That is, the word, or promise, that Christ should come into the world, 'who in the beginning was with God' — that is, it was in the purpose of God the Father to send God the Son into the world, to enlighten men in the way of eternal life; but it was not till then put into execution, and actually incarnate. So our Saviour is there called 'the Word' not because he was the promise, but the thing promised. Those who, taking occasion from this passage, commonly call him 'the Verbum of God,' do but render the text more obscure. They might as well call him the noun of God: for by noun, as also by verb, men understand nothing but a part of speech, a voice, a sound, that neither affirms nor denies, nor commands nor promises, nor is any substance corporeal or spiritual; and therefore it cannot be said to be either God or man — whereas our Saviour is both. And this Word, which St John in his Gospel says was with God, is (in his First Epistle, verse 1) called 'the Word of life'; and (verse 2) 'the eternal life, which was with the Father.' So he can in no other sense be called the Word than in the sense in which he is called eternal life — that is, 'he who has procured us eternal life,' by his coming in the flesh. So also (Revelation 19:13) the Apostle, speaking of Christ clothed in a garment dipped in blood, says his name is 'the Word of God' — which is to be understood as if he had said his name had been 'He that has come according to the purpose of God from the beginning, and according to his word and promises delivered by the prophets.' So there is nothing here of the incarnation of a Word, but of the incarnation of God the Son — therefore called the Word, because his incarnation was the performance of the promise; just as the Holy Ghost is called the Promise (Acts 1:4; Luke 24:49).

There are also passages of Scripture where, by the word of God, are signified such words as are consonant with reason and equity, though spoken sometimes neither by a prophet, nor by a holy man. For Pharaoh Necho was an idolater; yet his words to the good King Josiah, in which he advised him by messengers not to oppose his march against Carchemish, are said to have proceeded from the mouth of God; and that Josiah, not heeding them, was slain in the battle — as may be read in 2 Chron. 35:21–23. It is true that, as the same history is related in the first book of Esdras, it was not Pharaoh but Jeremiah who spoke these words to Josiah from the mouth of the Lord. But we are to give credit to the canonical Scripture, whatever is written in the Apocrypha.

The word of God is also to be taken for the dictates of reason and equity, when the same is said in the Scriptures to be written in man's heart; as in Psalm 36:31; Jeremiah 31:33; Deuteronomy 30:11, 14; and many other like passages.

The name PROPHET signifies in Scripture sometimes Prolocutor — that is, one who speaks from God to man, or from man to God; and sometimes Praedictor, or foreteller of things to come; and sometimes one who speaks incoherently, as men who are distracted. It is most frequently used in the sense of speaking from God to the people. So Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others were prophets. And in this sense the high priest was a prophet, for he alone went into the Sanctum Sanctorum to inquire of God, and was to declare God's answer to the people. So when Caiaphas said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, St John says (chapter 11:51) that 'he spoke not this of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that one man should die for the nation.' Also those who in Christian congregations taught the people (1 Cor. 14:3) are said to prophesy. In the like sense it is that God says to Moses (Exod. 4:16), concerning Aaron, 'He shall be your spokesman to the people; and he shall be to you a mouth, and you shall be to him in the place of God' — and what here is 'spokesman' is (chapter 7:1) interpreted as 'prophet': 'See (says God) I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.' In the sense of speaking from man to God, Abraham is called a prophet (Gen. 20:7), where God in a dream speaks to Abimelech in this way: 'Now therefore restore the man his wife, for he is a prophet, and shall pray for you' — whereby it may also be gathered that the name of prophet may not improperly be given to those who in Christian churches have a calling to say public prayers for the congregation. In the same sense, the prophets who came down from the high place (or hill of God) with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp (1 Sam. 10:5–6), and (verse 10) Saul among them, are said to prophesy, in that they praised God in that way publicly. In the like sense, Miriam is called a prophetess (Exod. 15:20). So it is also to be taken in 1 Cor. 11:4–5, where St Paul says, 'Every man that prays or prophesies with his head covered, etc., and every woman that prays or prophesies with her head uncovered' — for 'prophecy' in that place signifies nothing more than praising God in psalms and holy songs, which women might do in the church, though it were not lawful for them to speak to the congregation. And in this signification it is that the poets of the heathen, who composed hymns and other sorts of poems in honour of their gods, were called vates (prophets), as is well enough known by all who are versed in the books of the Gentiles, and as is evident in Titus 1:12, where St Paul says of the Cretans that a prophet of their own said they were liars — not that St Paul held their poets for prophets, but acknowledges that the word 'prophet' was commonly used to signify those who celebrated the honour of God in verse.

When by prophecy is meant prediction, or foretelling of future contingents, not only were those prophets who were God's spokesmen and foretold to others what God had foretold to them, but so also were all those impostors who claim by the help of familiar spirits, or by superstitious divination from past events with false causes, to foretell similar events in time to come; of which (as I have already declared in the 12th chapter of this discourse) there are many kinds, and who gain, in the opinion of the common sort of men, a greater reputation for prophecy by one chance event that may be wrested to their purpose than can be lost again by any number of failings. Prophecy is not an art, nor (when taken for prediction) a constant vocation, but an extraordinary and temporary employment from God, most often of good men, but sometimes also of the wicked. The woman of Endor, who is said to have had a familiar spirit, and thereby to have raised a phantasm of Samuel and foretold Saul his death, was not therefore a prophetess; for she had no science by which she could raise such a phantasm, nor does it appear that God commanded the raising of it. He only guided that imposture to be a means of Saul's terror and discouragement, and consequently of the rout by which he fell. And for incoherent speech, it was among the Gentiles taken for one kind of prophecy, because the prophets of their oracles, intoxicated with a spirit, or vapour from the cave of the Pythian oracle at Delphi, were for the time really mad, and spoke like madmen; out of whose loose words a sense might be made to fit any event, in such a way as all bodies are said to be made of materia prima. In Scripture I find it also so taken (1 Sam. 18:10) in these words: 'And the evil spirit came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house.'

And although there are so many meanings of the word 'prophet' in Scripture, the most frequent is that in which it is taken for the one to whom God speaks immediately what the prophet is to say from him, to some other man, or to the people. And on this a question may be asked: in what manner does God speak to such a prophet? Can it (some may say) be properly said that God has voice and language, when it cannot be properly said that he has a tongue, or other organs, as a man? The prophet David argues in this way: 'Shall he that made the eye not see? Or he that made the ear not hear?' But this may be spoken, not (as usually) to signify God's nature, but to signify our intention to honour him. For 'to see' and 'to hear' are honourable attributes, and may be given to God, to declare (as far as our capacity can conceive) his almighty power. But if it were taken in the strict and proper sense, one might argue, from his making of all parts of man's body, that he also has the same use of them that we have; which would be many of them so unseemly that it would be the greatest contumely in the world to ascribe them to him. We are therefore to interpret God's speaking to men immediately as the way (whatever it is) by which God makes them understand his will. And the ways by which he does this are many, and to be sought only in Holy Scripture. There, though many times it is said that God spoke to this or that person, without declaring in what manner, there are again many places that also give the signs by which they were to acknowledge his presence and commandment; and by these may be understood how he spoke to many of the rest.

In what manner God spoke to Adam, and Eve, and Cain, and Noah, is not expressed; nor how he spoke to Abraham, until the time when he came out of his own country to Shechem in the land of Canaan; and then (Gen. 12:7) God is said to have appeared to him. So there is one way by which God made his presence manifest: by an apparition, or vision. And again (Gen. 15:1), the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision — that is, something, as a sign of God's presence, appeared as God's messenger, to speak to him. Again, the Lord appeared to Abraham (Gen. 18:1) by an apparition of three angels; and to Abimelech (Gen. 20:3) in a dream; to Lot (Gen. 19:1) by an apparition of two angels; and to Hagar (Gen. 21:17) by the apparition of one angel; and to Abraham again (Gen. 22:11) by the apparition of a voice from heaven; and (Gen. 26:24) to Isaac in the night (that is, in his sleep, or by a dream); and to Jacob (Gen. 28:12) in a dream — that is (in the words of the text), 'Jacob dreamed that he saw a ladder, etc.' And (Gen. 32:1) in a vision of angels. And to Moses (Exod. 3:2) in the apparition of a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. And after the time of Moses, wherever the manner in which God spoke directly to a man in the Old Testament is expressed, he always spoke by a vision, or by a dream — as to Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the rest of the prophets; and often in the New Testament, as to Joseph, to St Peter, to St Paul, and to St John the Evangelist in the Apocalypse.

Only to Moses did he speak in a more extraordinary manner, on Mount Sinai and in the tabernacle; and to the high priest in the tabernacle, and in the Sanctum Sanctorum of the temple. But Moses, and after him the high priests, were prophets of a more eminent place and degree in God's favour. And God himself in express words declares that to other prophets he spoke in dreams and visions, but to his servant Moses, in such a manner as a man speaks to his friend. The words are these (Numb. 12:6–8): 'If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and will speak to him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all my house; with him I will speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the Lord shall he behold.' And (Exod. 33:11), 'The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' And yet this speaking of God to Moses was by the mediation of an angel, or angels, as appears expressly in Acts 7:35 and 53 and in Gal. 3:19; and was therefore a vision, though a clearer vision than was given to other prophets. And in keeping with this, where God says (Deut. 13:1), 'If there arise among you a prophet, or dreamer of dreams,' the latter word is only the interpretation of the former. And (Joel 2:28), 'Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions' — where again, the word 'prophecy' is expounded by 'dream' and 'vision.' And in the same way it was that God spoke to Solomon, promising him wisdom, riches, and honour; for the text says (1 Kings 3:15), 'And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream.' So that generally the prophets extraordinary in the Old Testament took notice of the word of God in no other way than from their dreams or visions — that is, from the imaginings they had in their sleep, or in an ecstasy. Which imaginings, in every true prophet, were supernatural; but in false prophets were either natural, or feigned.

The same prophets were nevertheless said to speak by the Spirit — as in Zechariah 7:12, where the prophet, speaking of the Jews, says: 'They made their hearts hard as adamant, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the Lord of hosts has sent in his Spirit by the former prophets.' By which it is plain that speaking by the Spirit, or inspiration, was not a particular manner of God's speaking, different from vision; when those who were said to speak by the Spirit were extraordinary prophets, such as had to have, for every new message, a particular commission — or (what is all one) a new dream, or vision.

To prophets of perpetual calling, and supreme, God spoke in the Old Testament from the mercy seat, in a manner not expressed in the Scripture. Of prophets who were so by a perpetual calling in the Old Testament, some were supreme and some subordinate. The supreme were first Moses; and after him the high priest, each one for his time, as long as the priesthood was royal. And after the people of the Jews had rejected God, that he should no more reign over them, those kings who submitted themselves to God's government were also his chief prophets; and the high priest's office became ministerial. When God was to be consulted, they put on the holy vestments and inquired of the Lord, as the king commanded them, and were deprived of their office when the king thought fit. For King Saul (1 Sam. 13:9) commanded the burnt offering to be brought; and (1 Sam. 14:18) he commands the priest to bring the ark near him, and (verse 19) again to let it alone, because he saw an advantage over his enemies. And in the same chapter Saul asks counsel of God. In the same way King David, after his being anointed, though before he had possession of the kingdom, is said to 'inquire of the Lord' (1 Sam. 23:2) whether he should fight against the Philistines at Keilah; and (verse 10) David commands the priest to bring him the ephod, to inquire whether he should stay in Keilah, or not. And King Solomon (1 Kings 2:27) took the priesthood from Abiathar, and gave it (verse 35) to Zadok. So Moses, and the high priests, and the pious kings who inquired of God on all extraordinary occasions how they were to conduct themselves, or what outcome they were to have, were all sovereign prophets. But in what manner God spoke to them is not plain. To say that when Moses went up to God on Mount Sinai, it was a dream, or vision, such as other prophets had, is contrary to the distinction God made between Moses and other prophets (Numb. 12:6–8). To say God spoke or appeared as he is in his own nature is to deny his infiniteness, invisibility, incomprehensibility. To say he spoke by inspiration, or infusion, of the Holy Spirit — as the Holy Spirit signifies the Deity — is to make Moses equal with Christ, in whom alone the Godhead (as St Paul says, Col. 2:9) 'dwells bodily.' And lastly, to say he spoke by the Holy Spirit, as it signifies the graces or gifts of the Holy Spirit, is to attribute nothing supernatural to him. For God disposes men to piety, justice, mercy, truth, faith, and every kind of virtue — moral and intellectual — by doctrine, example, and various occasions, natural and ordinary.

And as these ways cannot be applied to God in his speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, so they cannot be applied to him in his speaking to the high priests from the mercy seat. So in what manner God spoke to those sovereign prophets of the Old Testament, whose office it was to inquire of him, is not intelligible. In the time of the New Testament there was no sovereign prophet but our Saviour, who was both God who spoke, and the prophet to whom he spoke.

To prophets of perpetual calling but subordinate, God spoke by the Spirit. To subordinate prophets of perpetual calling, I find no place that proves God spoke to them supernaturally, but only in such a manner as he naturally inclines men to piety, to belief, to righteousness, and to other virtues — all other Christian men. Which way, though it consists in constitution, instruction, education, and the occasions and inducements men have to Christian virtues, is yet truly attributed to the operation of the Spirit of God, or the Holy Spirit (which in our language we call the Holy Ghost); for there is no good inclination that is not from the operation of God. But these operations are not always supernatural. So when a prophet is said to speak in the Spirit, or by the Spirit of God, we are to understand no more than that he speaks according to God's will, declared by the supreme prophet. For the most common acceptation of the word 'spirit' is in the sense of a man's intention, mind, or disposition.

In the time of Moses there were seventy men besides himself who prophesied in the camp of the Israelites. In what manner God spoke to them is declared in Numbers 11:25: 'The Lord came down in a cloud, and spoke to Moses, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it to the seventy elders. And it came to pass, when the spirit rested on them, they prophesied, and did not cease.' By which it is plain, first, that their prophesying to the people was subservient and subordinate to the prophesying of Moses; for God took of the spirit of Moses to put on them, so that they prophesied as Moses would have them — otherwise they had not been allowed to prophesy at all. For there was (verse 27) a complaint made against them to Moses, and Joshua would have had Moses forbid them; which Moses did not, but said to Joshua, 'Be not jealous on my behalf.' Second, that the Spirit of God in that place signifies nothing but the mind and disposition to obey, and to assist Moses, in the administration of the government. For if it were meant that they had the substantial Spirit of God — that is, the divine nature, inspired into them — then they had it no less than Christ himself, in whom alone the Spirit of God dwelt bodily. It is meant therefore of the gift and grace of God, that guided them to co-operate with Moses, from whom their spirit was derived. And it appears (verse 16) that they were such as Moses himself should appoint for elders and officers of the people; for the words are, 'Gather to me seventy men, whom you know to be elders and officers of the people' — where 'you know' is the same as 'you appoint,' or 'have appointed to be such.' For we are told before (Exod. 18) that Moses, following the counsel of Jethro his father-in-law, appointed judges and officers over the people, such as feared God; and of these were those seventy whom God, by putting Moses' spirit on them, inclined to aid Moses in the administration of the kingdom. And in this sense the Spirit of God is said (1 Sam. 16:13–14), immediately on the anointing of David, to have come on David, and left Saul — God giving his graces to him whom he chose to govern his people, and taking them away from the one he rejected. So that by 'the Spirit' is meant inclination to God's service, and not any supernatural revelation.

God also spoke many times by the outcome of lots, which were ordered by such as he had put in authority over his people. So we read that God made known, by the lots Saul caused to be drawn (1 Sam. 14:43), the fault that Jonathan had committed in eating a honeycomb, contrary to the oath taken by the people. And (Josh. 18:10), God divided the land of Canaan among the Israelites by the 'lots that Joshua cast before the Lord in Shiloh.' In the same way it seems to be that God discovered (Joshua 7:16, etc.) the crime of Achan. And these are the ways by which God declared his will in the Old Testament.

All these ways he used also in the New Testament. To the Virgin Mary, by a vision of an angel; to Joseph in a dream; again to Paul on the way to Damascus, in a vision of our Saviour; and to Peter in the vision of a sheet let down from heaven with various sorts of flesh, of clean and unclean beasts, and in prison by the vision of an angel; and to all the apostles, and writers of the New Testament, by the graces of his Spirit; and to the apostles again (at the choosing of Matthias in the place of Judas Iscariot) by lot.

Since then all prophecy supposes vision, or dream (which two, when they are natural, are the same), or some special gift of God so rarely seen in mankind as to be admired where seen; and since both such gifts and the most extraordinary dreams and visions may proceed from God, not only by his supernatural and immediate operation, but also by his natural operation, and through the mediation of secondary causes — there is need of reason and judgement to discern between natural and supernatural gifts, and between natural and supernatural visions or dreams. And consequently men have need to be very circumspect and wary in obeying the voice of a man who, claiming to be a prophet, requires us to obey God in the way that he, in God's name, tells us is the way to happiness. For he who claims to teach men the way to so great a felicity claims to govern them — that is, to rule and reign over them; which is a thing that all men naturally desire, and is therefore to be suspected of ambition and imposture; and consequently ought to be examined, and tested, by every man before he yields them obedience — unless he has yielded it to them already, in the institution of a commonwealth, as when the prophet is the civil sovereign, or is authorised by the civil sovereign. And if this examination of prophets and spirits were not allowed to every one of the people, it would have been to no purpose to set out the marks by which every man might be able to distinguish between those he ought, and those he ought not, to follow. Since therefore such marks are set out (Deut. 13:1ff.) to know a prophet by, and (1 John 4:1ff.) to know a spirit by; and since there is so much prophesying in the Old Testament, and so much preaching in the New Testament against prophets; and so much greater a number ordinarily of false prophets than of true — every one is to beware of obeying their directions, at his own peril. And first, that there were many more false than true prophets appears from this, that when Ahab (1 Kings 22 [which Hobbes here numbers as 12]) consulted four hundred prophets, they were all false impostors, except only one — Micaiah. And a little before the time of the captivity, the prophets were generally liars. 'The prophets,' says the Lord through Jeremiah 14:14, 'prophesy lies in my name. I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, nor spoken to them; they prophesy to you a false vision, a thing of naught, and the deceit of their heart.' So much so that God commanded the people, by the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah (chapter 23:16), not to obey them: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: listen not to the words of the prophets that prophesy to you. They make you vain; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the Lord.'

Since, then, there was in the time of the Old Testament such quarrelling among the visionary prophets — one contesting with another, and asking 'When did the Spirit depart from me, to go to you?' as between Micaiah and the rest of the four hundred; and such giving of the lie to one another (as in Jeremiah 14:14); and such controversies, in the New Testament and at this day, among the spiritual prophets — every man then was, and now is, bound to make use of his natural reason, to apply to all prophecy the rules God has given us to discern the true from the false. Of which rules, in the Old Testament one was the conformity of doctrine to what Moses the sovereign prophet had taught them, and the other the miraculous power of foretelling what God would bring to pass, as I have already shown out of Deut. 13:1ff. And in the New Testament there was only one mark, and that was the preaching of this doctrine: that Jesus is the Christ — that is, the king of the Jews, promised in the Old Testament. Whoever denied that article was a false prophet, whatever miracles he might seem to work; and he who taught it was a true prophet. For St John (1 Epistle 4:2ff.), speaking expressly of the means to examine spirits, whether they are of God or not — after he has told them that there would arise false prophets — says: 'Hereby know the Spirit of God. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God' — that is, is approved and allowed as a prophet of God; not that he is a godly man, or one of the elect, just because he confesses, professes, or preaches Jesus to be the Christ, but that he is an avowed prophet. For God sometimes speaks by prophets whose persons he has not accepted, as he did by Balaam; and as he foretold Saul of his death, by the witch of Endor. Again in the next verse: 'Every spirit that confesses not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, is not of Christ. And this is the spirit of antichrist.' So the rule is perfect on both sides: that he is a true prophet who preaches the Messiah already come, in the person of Jesus; and a false one who denies him come, and looks for him in some future impostor who will take that honour on himself falsely — whom the apostle there properly calls antichrist. Every man therefore ought to consider who is the sovereign prophet — that is, who it is that is God's viceregent on earth, and has, next under God, the authority of governing Christian men; and to observe as a rule that doctrine which, in the name of God, he commands to be taught; and by this to examine and try out the truth of those doctrines which pretended prophets, with miracles or without, may at any time advance. And if they find it contrary to that rule, to do as those did who came to Moses and complained that there were some who prophesied in the camp, whose authority so to do they doubted; and leave it to the sovereign, as they did to Moses, to uphold them or to forbid them as he shall see cause; and if he disavows them, then no more to obey their voice; or if he approves them, then to obey them, as men to whom God has given a part of the spirit of their sovereign. For when Christian men do not take their Christian sovereign for God's prophet, they must either take their own dreams for the prophecy they mean to be governed by, and the swelling of their own hearts for the Spirit of God; or they must suffer themselves to be led by some strange prince, or by some of their fellow subjects, that can bewitch them, by slander of the government, into rebellion, without other miracle to confirm their calling than sometimes an extraordinary success, and impunity. And by this means, destroying all laws both divine and human, they reduce all order, government, and society to the first chaos of violence and civil war.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVII. Of Miracles, and Their Use
paragraphs: By MIRACLES are signified the admirable works of God; and so they are also called wonders. And because they are for the most part done as a signification of his commandment — on such occasions as, without them, men are apt to doubt (following their private natural reasoning) what he has commanded and what he has not — they are commonly called in Holy Scripture signs, in the same sense as they are called by the Latins ostenta and portenta, from the showing and the foresignifying of what the Almighty is about to bring to pass.

To understand, then, what a miracle is, we must first understand what kinds of works men wonder at and call admirable. There are only two things that make men wonder at any event. One is, if it is strange — that is, such as the like has never, or very rarely, been produced. The other is, if when it is produced, we cannot imagine it to have been done by natural means, but only by the immediate hand of God. But when we see some possible natural cause of it, however rarely the like has been done, or if the like has often been done however impossible it may be to imagine a natural means for it, we no longer wonder, nor count it for a miracle.

So if a horse, or a cow, should speak, it would be a miracle, because the thing is strange and a natural cause is hard to imagine; so too would it be to see a strange deviation of nature in the production of some new shape of a living creature. But when a man, or other animal, begets his like, then, though we know no more of how this is done than of the other, since it is usual it is no miracle. In the same way, if a man is metamorphosed into a stone, or into a pillar, it is a miracle, because strange; but if a piece of wood is so changed, since we see it often, it is no miracle — and yet we know no more, by what operation of God the one is brought to pass than the other.

The first rainbow ever seen in the world was a miracle, because it was the first, and so strange, and served as a sign from God placed in heaven, to assure his people that there should be no more a universal destruction of the world by water. But today, because rainbows are frequent, they are not miracles, neither to those who know their natural causes, nor to those who do not. Again, there are many rare works produced by the art of man; yet when we know they are done — because by that we know also the means by which they are done — we do not count them for miracles, because they are not wrought by the immediate hand of God, but by the mediation of human industry.
What seems a miracle to one man may seem otherwise to another.

Furthermore, since admiration and wonder are consequent on the knowledge and experience with which men are endowed — some more, some less — it follows that the same thing may be a miracle to one and not to another. From this it comes that ignorant and superstitious men make great wonders of works that other men, knowing they proceed from nature (which is not the immediate, but the ordinary, work of God), do not admire at all: as when eclipses of the sun and moon have been taken for supernatural works by the common people, when nevertheless there were others who, from their natural causes, could have foretold the very hour at which they would happen. Or as when a man, by confederacy and secret intelligence, gets knowledge of the private actions of an ignorant, unwary man, and thereby tells him what he has done in former time — it seems to him a miraculous thing; but among wise, and cautious, men such miracles as these cannot easily be done.

Again, it belongs to the nature of a miracle that it be wrought to procure credit for God's messengers, ministers, and prophets — so that men may know they are called, sent, and employed by God, and thereby be the better inclined to obey them. And so, though the creation of the world, and afterwards the destruction of all living creatures in the universal deluge, were admirable works, they are not usually called miracles, because they were not done to procure credit for any prophet or other minister of God. For however admirable any work is, the admiration consists not in that it could be done — for men naturally believe the Almighty can do all things — but in that he does it at the prayer, or word, of a man. But the works of God in Egypt, by the hand of Moses, were properly miracles, because they were done with the intention of making the people of Israel believe that Moses came to them, not out of any design of his own interest, but as sent from God. So after God had commanded him to deliver the Israelites from the Egyptian bondage, when Moses said (Exod. 4:1 etc.), 'They will not believe me, but will say, The Lord has not appeared to me,' God gave him power to turn the rod he had in his hand into a serpent, and again to turn it back into a rod; and, by putting his hand into his bosom, to make it leprous, and again, by pulling it out, to make it whole — to make the children of Israel believe (as it is verse 5) that the God of their fathers had appeared to him. And if that were not enough, he gave him power to turn their waters into blood. And when he had done these miracles before the people, it is said (verse 41 [verse 31]) that 'they believed him.' Nevertheless, for fear of Pharaoh, they did not yet dare to obey him. So the other works which were done to plague Pharaoh and the Egyptians all tended to make the Israelites believe in Moses, and were properly miracles. In the same way, if we consider all the miracles done by the hand of Moses, and of all the rest of the prophets, until the captivity; and those of our Saviour, and his apostles afterwards — we shall find that their end was always to beget, or confirm, the belief that they did not come on their own motion, but were sent by God. We may further note in Scripture that the end of miracles was to beget belief, not universally in all men, elect and reprobate, but in the elect only — that is, in such as God had determined should become his subjects. For those miraculous plagues of Egypt did not have for their end the conversion of Pharaoh; for God had told Moses beforehand that he would harden the heart of Pharaoh, that he should not let the people go. And when at last he did let them go, it was not the miracles that persuaded him, but the plagues that forced him to it. So also of our Saviour it is written (Matt. 13:58) that he wrought not many miracles in his own country because of their unbelief; and (in Mark 6:5), instead of 'he wrought not many,' it is 'he could work none.' It was not that he lacked power — to say this would be blasphemy against God; nor that the end of miracles was not to convert incredulous men to Christ, for the end of all the miracles of Moses, of the prophets, of our Saviour, and of his apostles was to add men to the Church. It was because the end of their miracles was to add to the Church not all men, but such as should be saved — that is, such as God had elected. Since therefore our Saviour was sent from his Father, he could not use his power in the conversion of those whom his Father had rejected. Those who, expounding this passage of St Mark, say that his word 'he could not' is put for 'he would not,' do this without any example in the Greek tongue (where 'would not' is sometimes put for 'could not' in inanimate things which have no will, but 'could not' for 'would not' is never put), and so lay a stumbling-block before weak Christians, as if Christ could do no miracles except among the credulous.

From what I have set down here concerning the nature and use of a miracle, we may define it thus: 'A MIRACLE is a work of God (besides his operation by the way of nature, ordained in the creation) done for the making manifest to his elect of the mission of an extraordinary minister for their salvation.'

And from this definition we may infer, first, that in all miracles the work done is not the effect of any power in the prophet, because it is the effect of the immediate hand of God — that is, God has done it without using the prophet in it as a subordinate cause.

Second, that no devil, angel, or other created spirit can do a miracle. For it must be either by virtue of some natural science, or by incantation — that is, by virtue of words. For if the enchanters do it by their own power independent of God, there is some power that does not proceed from God, which all men deny; and if they do it by power given to them, then the work is not from the immediate hand of God, but natural — and consequently no miracle.

There are some texts of Scripture that seem to attribute the power of working wonders (equal to some of those immediate miracles wrought by God himself) to certain arts of magic, and incantation. For example, when we read that, after the rod of Moses, being cast on the ground, became a serpent, 'the magicians of Egypt did the like by their enchantments' (Exod. 7:11); and that after Moses had turned the waters of the Egyptian streams, rivers, ponds, and pools of water into blood, 'the magicians of Egypt did so likewise, with their enchantments' (Exod. 7:22); and that, after Moses had by the power of God brought frogs upon the land, 'the magicians also did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt' (Exod. 8:7) — will not a man be apt to attribute miracles to enchantments — that is, to the efficacy of the sound of words — and think the same very well proved from this and other such passages? And yet there is no passage of Scripture that tells us what an enchantment is. So if enchantment is not, as many think it, the working of strange effects by spells and words, but imposture and delusion wrought by ordinary means — and so far from being supernatural that the impostors do not need so much as a study of natural causes, but only the ordinary ignorance, stupidity, and superstition of mankind to do them — then those texts that seem to countenance the power of magic, witchcraft, and enchantment must have a sense other than they seem at first sight to bear.

For it is plain enough that words have no effect except on those who understand them; and then they have no other effect but to signify the intentions or passions of those who speak, and thereby produce hope, fear, or other passions or conceptions in the hearer. So when a rod seems a serpent, or water blood, or any other miracle seems to be done by enchantment — if it is not for the edification of God's people — then neither the rod, nor the water, nor any other thing is enchanted, that is, wrought upon by the words; the spectator is. So all the miracle consists in this, that the enchanter has deceived a man — which is no miracle, but a very easy matter to do.

For such is the ignorance, and aptness to error, generally of all men — but especially of those who have little knowledge of natural causes, and of the nature and interests of men — that they may be misled by countless and easy tricks. What opinion of miraculous power, before it was known there is a science of the course of the stars, might a man have gained who told the people, 'At this hour, or day, the sun shall be darkened'? A juggler, by the handling of his cups and other trinkets, if it were not now commonly practised, would be thought to do his wonders at least by the power of the devil. A man who has practised to speak by drawing in his breath (which kind of men in ancient times were called ventriloqui), and so to make the weakness of his voice seem to proceed not from the weak impulsion of the organs of speech, but from distance of place, is able to make a great many men believe it is a voice from heaven, whatever he pleases to tell them. And for a cunning man who has inquired into the secrets and familiar confessions that one man ordinarily makes to another of his past actions and adventures, to tell them back to him is no hard matter; and yet there are many who by such means as this gain the reputation of being conjurers. But it would take too long to list all the various sorts of those men whom the Greeks called Thaumaturgi — that is, workers of wonderful things — and yet these do all they do by their own single dexterity. But if we look at the impostures wrought by confederacy, there is nothing, however impossible to be done, that is impossible to be believed. For two men conspiring, one to seem lame and the other to cure him with a charm, will deceive many; but many conspiring — one to seem lame, another so to cure him, and all the rest to bear witness — will deceive many more.

In this aptness of mankind to give too hasty belief to pretended miracles, there can be no better, nor (I think) any other, precaution than the one which God has prescribed, first by Moses (as I have said before in the previous chapter), at the beginning of Deuteronomy 13 and at the end of Deuteronomy 18: that we take none for prophets who teach any other religion than the one which God's lieutenant (who at that time was Moses) has established, nor any (even if he teaches the same religion) whose prediction we do not see come to pass. So Moses in his time, and Aaron and his successors in their times, and the sovereign governor of God's people, next under God himself — that is, the head of the church at all times — are to be consulted as to what doctrine he has established, before we give credit to a pretended miracle or prophet. And when that is done, the thing they claim to be a miracle we must both see done, and use all possible means to consider whether it is really done; and not only so, but whether it is such as no man can do the like by his natural power, but that it requires the immediate hand of God. And in this also we must have recourse to God's lieutenant, to whom in all doubtful cases we have submitted our private judgements. For example: if a man claims that after certain words spoken over a piece of bread, God has at once made it not bread, but a god, or a man, or both — and nevertheless it still looks as like bread as ever it did — there is no reason for any man to think it really done; nor, consequently, to fear him, till he inquires of God, by his vicar or lieutenant, whether it is done or not. If he says no, then follows what Moses says (Deut. 18:22): 'He has spoken it presumptuously; you shall not fear him.' If he says it is done, then he is not to be contradicted. So also if we do not see, but only hear tell of, a miracle, we are to consult the lawful church — that is, the lawful head of it — as to how far we are to give credit to those who report it. And this is chiefly the case of men who in these days live under Christian sovereigns. For in these times, I do not know of one man who ever saw any such wonderful work done by the charm, or at the word, or prayer of a man, that a man endowed with even a mediocrity of reason would think supernatural. And the question is no longer whether what we see done is a miracle, or whether the miracle we hear, or read of, was a real work and not the act of a tongue or a pen; but in plain terms, whether the report is true or a lie. In this question we are not each of us to make our own private reason, or conscience, the judge, but the public reason — that is, the reason of God's supreme lieutenant — is judge; and indeed we have made him judge already, if we have given him a sovereign power to do all that is necessary for our peace and defence. A private man has always the liberty (because thought is free) to believe, or not believe, in his heart those acts which have been given out for miracles, according as he shall see what benefit may come, by men's belief, to those who claim or countenance them, and thereby conjecture whether they are miracles or lies. But when it comes to the confession of that faith, the private reason must submit to the public — that is, to God's lieutenant. But who this lieutenant of God, and head of the church, is, shall be considered in its proper place hereafter.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVIII. Of the Signification in Scripture of Eternall Life, Hell, Salvation, the World to Come, and Redemption
paragraphs: The maintenance of civil society depends on justice; and justice depends on the power of life and death, and on other lesser rewards and punishments, residing in those who have the sovereignty of the commonwealth. It is impossible that a commonwealth should stand where any other than the sovereign has the power of giving greater rewards than life, and of inflicting greater punishments than death. Now since eternal life is a greater reward than the present life, and eternal torment a greater punishment than the death of nature, it is a thing worth carefully considering — by all men who desire (by obeying authority) to avoid the calamities of confusion and civil war — what is meant in Holy Scripture by 'life eternal' and 'torment eternal'; and for what offences, and against whom committed, men are to be eternally tormented; and for what actions, they are to obtain eternal life.
The place of Adam's eternity, if he had not sinned: the terrestrial paradise.

And first we find that Adam was created in such a state of life that, had he not broken the commandment of God, he would have enjoyed it in the paradise of Eden everlastingly. For there was the tree of life, of which he was allowed to eat so long as he should forbear to eat of the tree of knowledge of good and evil — which was not allowed him. And so as soon as he had eaten of it, God thrust him out of paradise, 'lest he should put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever' (Gen. 3:22). By this it seems to me — with submission, nevertheless, both on this and on all questions whose determination depends on the Scriptures, to the interpretation of the Bible authorised by the commonwealth, whose subject I am — that Adam, had he not sinned, would have had an eternal life on earth, and that mortality entered upon himself and his posterity by his first sin. Not that actual death then entered: for Adam then could never have had children, whereas he lived long after, and saw a numerous posterity before he died. But where it is said, 'In the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die,' it must be meant of his mortality, and the certitude of death. Since then eternal life was lost by Adam's forfeiture, in committing sin, he who should cancel that forfeiture was to recover by that means the same life. Now Jesus Christ has satisfied for the sins of all who believe in him, and so has recovered to all believers that ETERNAL LIFE which was lost by the sin of Adam. And in this sense the comparison of St Paul holds (Rom. 5:18–19): 'As by the offence of one, judgement came on all men to condemnation, even so by the righteousness of one, the free gift came on all men to justification of life.' Which is again (1 Cor. 15:21–22) more clearly delivered in these words: 'For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.'

Concerning the place where men shall enjoy that eternal life which Christ has obtained for them, the texts just cited seem to make it on earth. For if, as in Adam all die — that is, have forfeited paradise and eternal life on earth — even so in Christ all shall be made alive, then all men shall be made to live on earth; for otherwise the comparison would not be proper. With this seems to agree the saying of the Psalmist (Ps. 133:3): 'Upon Zion God commanded the blessing, even life for evermore'; for Zion is in Jerusalem, on earth. As also the saying of St John (Rev. 2:7): 'To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.' This was the tree of Adam's eternal life; but his life was to have been on earth. The same seems to be confirmed again by St John (Rev. 21:2), where he says: 'I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband'; and again at verse 10, to the same effect — as if he should say, the new Jerusalem, the paradise of God, at the coming again of Christ, should come down to God's people from heaven, and not they go up to it from earth. And this differs not at all from what the two men in white clothing (that is, the two angels) said to the apostles, who were looking on Christ ascending (Acts 1:11): 'This same Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come, as you have seen him go up into heaven.' Which sounds as if they had said that he should come down to govern them under his Father, eternally, here — not take them up to govern them in heaven; and is in keeping with the restoration of the kingdom of God, instituted under Moses, which was a political government of the Jews on earth. Again, that saying of our Saviour (Matt. 22:30), 'that in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven,' is a description of an eternal life resembling what we lost in Adam, on the point of marriage. For since Adam and Eve, had they not sinned, would have lived on earth eternally in their individual persons, it is plain they should not have continually procreated their kind. For if immortals had generated as mankind does now, the earth in a small time would not be able to afford them a place to stand on. The Jews who asked our Saviour the question — whose wife the woman who had married many brothers should be in the resurrection — did not know the consequences of immortality: that there shall be no generation, and consequently no marriage, any more than there is marriage, or generation, among the angels. The comparison between that eternal life which Adam lost, and what our Saviour by his victory over death has recovered, holds also in this: that as Adam lost eternal life by his sin, and yet lived after it for a time, so the faithful Christian has recovered eternal life by Christ's passion, even though he dies a natural death, and remains dead for a time — namely, till the resurrection. For as death is reckoned from the condemnation of Adam, not from the execution; so life is reckoned from the absolution, not from the resurrection, of those who are elected in Christ.

That the place where men are to live eternally, after the resurrection, is the heavens — meaning by 'heaven' those parts of the world most remote from earth, where the stars are, or above the stars in another, higher, heaven called Caelum Empyreum (of which there is no mention in Scripture, nor ground in reason) — is not easily to be drawn from any text I can find. By 'the kingdom of heaven' is meant the kingdom of the king who dwells in heaven; and his kingdom was the people of Israel, whom he ruled by the prophets, his lieutenants — first Moses, and after him Eleazar, and the sovereign priests — until in the days of Samuel they rebelled and would have a mortal man for their king, after the manner of other nations. And when our Saviour Christ, by the preaching of his ministers, shall have persuaded the Jews to return, and called the Gentiles to his obedience, then shall there be a new kingdom of heaven, because our king shall then be God, whose throne is heaven — without any necessity evident in Scripture that man shall ascend to his happiness any higher than God's footstool, the earth. On the contrary, we find written (John 3:13) that 'no man has ascended into heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man, that is in heaven.' Where I observe in passing that these words are not, like those immediately before, the words of our Saviour, but of St John himself; for Christ was then not in heaven, but on the earth. The like is said of David (Acts 2:34), where St Peter, to prove the ascension of Christ, using the words of the Psalmist (Ps. 16:10), 'You will not leave my soul in hell, nor allow your Holy One to see corruption,' says they were spoken not of David, but of Christ; and to prove it, adds this reason: 'For David is not ascended into heaven.' But to this a man may easily answer, and say, that though their bodies were not to ascend until the general day of judgement, yet their souls were in heaven as soon as they were departed from their bodies. Which also seems to be confirmed by the words of our Saviour (Luke 20:37–38), who, proving the resurrection out of the word of Moses, says: 'That the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living, for they all live to him.' But if these words are to be understood only of the immortality of the soul, they do not prove at all what our Saviour intended to prove — which was the resurrection of the body, that is, the immortality of the man. So our Saviour means that those patriarchs were immortal, not by a property consequent on the essence and nature of mankind, but by the will of God, who was pleased of his mere grace to bestow eternal life on the faithful. And though at that time the patriarchs, and many other faithful men, were dead, yet, as it is in the text, they 'lived to God' — that is, they were written in the Book of Life with those who were absolved of their sins, and ordained to life eternal at the resurrection. That the soul of man is in its own nature eternal, and a living creature independent of the body — or that any mere man is immortal, otherwise than by the resurrection on the last day (except Enoch and Elijah) — is a doctrine not apparent in Scripture. The whole 14th chapter of Job, which is the speech not of his friends but of himself, is a complaint of this mortality of nature, and yet no contradiction of immortality at the resurrection. 'There is hope of a tree,' he says (verse 7), 'if it be cast down, that though the root of it grows old, and the stock of it dies in the ground, yet when it scents the water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dies, and wastes away — yea, man gives up the ghost, and where is he?' And (verse 12), 'Man lies down, and rises not, till the heavens be no more.' But when is it that the heavens shall be no more? St Peter tells us it is at the general resurrection. For in his second Epistle, chapter 3, verse 7, he says, 'The heavens and the earth that are now are reserved to fire, against the day of judgement and perdition of ungodly men'; and (verse 12), 'looking for, and hastening to, the coming of God, in which the heavens shall be on fire, and shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat. Nevertheless, we, according to the promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, in which dwells righteousness.' So where Job says man does not rise till the heavens be no more, it is all one as if he had said, the immortal life (and 'soul' and 'life' in Scripture usually mean the same thing) does not begin in man until the resurrection and the day of judgement; and has for its cause not his specific nature and generation, but the promise. For St Peter does not say 'We look for new heavens and a new earth (from nature),' but 'from promise.'

Lastly, since it has already been proved out of various plain places of Scripture, in the 35th chapter of this book, that the kingdom of God is a civil commonwealth in which God himself is sovereign, by virtue first of the Old and then of the New Covenant, in which he reigns by his vicar or lieutenant — the same passages therefore also prove that, after the coming again of our Saviour in his majesty and glory, to reign actually and eternally, the kingdom of God is to be on earth. But because this doctrine (though proved from passages of Scripture neither few nor obscure) will seem to most men a novelty, I only put it forward, maintaining nothing in this, or in any other paradox of religion, but waiting for the end of that dispute of the sword concerning the authority (not yet decided among my countrymen) by which all kinds of doctrine are to be approved, or rejected; and whose commands, both in speech and in writing (whatever the opinions of private men may be), must be obeyed by all who mean to be protected by their laws. For the points of doctrine concerning the kingdom of God have so great an influence on the kingdom of man as not to be determined except by those who, under God, have the sovereign power.
The place after judgement of those who were never in the kingdom of God, or, having been in, are cast out.

As the kingdom of God, and eternal life, so also God's enemies and their torments after judgement appear by Scripture to have their place on earth. The name of the place where all men remain till the resurrection — those who were either buried, or swallowed up by the earth — is usually called in Scripture by words that signify 'under ground'; which the Latins generally read as Infernus and Inferni, and the Greeks Hades — that is, a place where men cannot see; and it includes the grave as well as any deeper place. But for the place of the damned after the resurrection, it is not determined either in the Old or in the New Testament by any note of location, but only by the company; as that it shall be where such wicked men were as God had in former times in an extraordinary and miraculous manner destroyed from off the face of the earth. As, for example, that they are in Inferno, in Tartarus, or in the bottomless pit, because Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were swallowed up alive into the earth. Not that the writers of Scripture would have us believe there could be in the globe of the earth — which is not only finite, but also (compared to the height of the stars) of no considerable size — a pit without a bottom, that is, a hole of infinite depth, such as the Greeks in their daemonology (their doctrine concerning daemons), and after them the Romans, called Tartarus; of which Virgil says:
Bis patet in praeceps, tantum tenditque sub umbras, / Quantus ad aethereum coeli suspectus Olympum.

For that is a thing the proportion of earth to heaven cannot bear. But rather that we should believe them to be there indefinitely — where those men are on whom God inflicted that exemplary punishment.

Again, because those mighty men of the earth who lived in the time of Noah, before the flood (which the Greeks called Heroes, and the Scripture Giants — and both say were begotten by the copulation of the children of God with the children of men), were destroyed for their wicked life by the general deluge, the place of the damned is therefore also sometimes marked out by the company of those deceased giants. As Proverbs 21:16: 'The man that wanders out of the way of understanding shall remain in the congregation of the giants.' And Job 26:5: 'Behold the giants groan under water, and they that dwell with them.' Here the place of the damned is under the water. And Isaiah 14:9: 'Hell is troubled how to meet you' (that is, the king of Babylon), 'and will displace the giants for you' — and here again the place of the damned (if the sense is literal) is to be under water.

Third, because the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, by the extraordinary wrath of God, were consumed for their wickedness with fire and brimstone, and together with them the country around them made a stinking bituminous lake, the place of the damned is sometimes expressed by fire, and a fiery lake. As in the Apocalypse 21:8: 'But the timorous, incredulous, and abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death.' So that it is plain that 'hellfire,' which is here expressed by metaphor from the real fire of Sodom, signifies no particular kind, or place, of torment, but is to be taken indefinitely for destruction — as it is in the 20th chapter, at the 14th verse, where it is said that 'death and hell were cast into the lake of fire' — that is, were abolished and destroyed; as if after the day of judgement there shall be no more dying, nor any more going into hell — that is, no more going to Hades (from which word our word 'hell' is perhaps derived), which is the same as no more dying.

Fourth, from the plague of darkness inflicted on the Egyptians, of which it is written (Exod. 10:23), 'They saw not one another, neither did any man rise from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings,' the place of the wicked after judgement is called 'outer darkness' — or (as it is in the original) 'darkness without.' And so it is expressed (Matt. 22:13), where the king commands his servants 'to bind hand and foot the man that had not on his wedding garment, and to cast him out' — eis to skotos to exoteron, external darkness, or 'darkness without': which, though translated 'outer darkness,' does not signify how great, but where, that darkness is to be — namely, outside the habitation of God's elect.

Lastly, whereas there was a place near Jerusalem called the Valley of the Children of Hinnom — in a part of which, called Tophet, the Jews had committed most grievous idolatry, sacrificing their children to the idol Moloch; and in which also God had afflicted his enemies with most grievous punishments; and in which Josiah had burnt the priests of Moloch on their own altars, as appears at large in 2 Kings chapter 23 — that place served afterwards to receive the filth and garbage which was carried there out of the city; and there fires used to be made, from time to time, to purify the air and take away the stench of carrion. From this abominable place, the Jews used ever after to call the place of the damned by the name of Gehenna, or Valley of Hinnom. And this Gehenna is the word that is usually now translated HELL; and from the fires from time to time burning there, we get the notion of 'everlasting and unquenchable fire.'

Since now there is no one who so interprets the Scripture as that after the day of judgement the wicked are all eternally to be punished in the Valley of Hinnom; or that they shall so rise again as to be ever after under ground, or under water; or that after the resurrection they shall no more see one another, nor stir from one place to another — it follows, it seems to me, very necessarily that what is thus said concerning hellfire is spoken metaphorically; and that therefore there is a proper sense to be inquired after (for of all metaphors there is some real ground that may be expressed in proper words), both of the place of hell, and of the nature of hellish torment and tormentors.

And first, for the tormentors, we have their nature and properties exactly and properly delivered by the names of The Enemy, or Satan; The Accuser, or Diabolus; The Destroyer, or Abaddon. Which significant names — Satan, Devil, Abaddon — set forth to us no individual person, as proper names usually do, but only an office, or quality; and are therefore appellatives, which ought not to have been left untranslated, as they are, in the Latin and modern Bibles. For thereby they seem to be the proper names of daemons; and men are the more easily seduced to believe the doctrine of devils — which at that time was the religion of the Gentiles, and contrary to that of Moses, and of Christ.

And because by the Enemy, the Accuser, and the Destroyer is meant the enemy of those who shall be in the kingdom of God, therefore if the kingdom of God after the resurrection is on earth (as in the previous chapter I have shown by Scripture it seems to be), the Enemy, and his kingdom, must be on earth also. For so it was in the time before the Jews had deposed God. For God's kingdom was in Palestine, and the nations round about were the kingdoms of the Enemy; and consequently by 'Satan' is meant any earthly enemy of the church.
